MR. BROADBENT-ALLEGED FAILURE TO INVESTIGATE AUTOMOBILE PRICE INCREASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. Late in the last session of Parliament the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs asserted that if the automobile companies introduced a substantial increase in the price of their 1970 models he would undertake an investigation of their pricing policies. Yesterday in the House, when I asked what had been done by the minister since the automobile manufacturers announced higher prices for their new 1970 models, he reneged on this commitment to the people of Canada.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, if you agree with me I should like to move that this matter be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. BROADBENT-ALLEGED FAILURE TO INVESTIGATE AUTOMOBILE PRICE INCREASES
speechtext:
Order, please. I notice that the President of the Privy Council wishes to rise in connection with the point raised by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby. As he knows, by virtue of the Standing Order the hon. member is required to give notice, which he has done, to give the Chair an opportunity to study the matter extensively, which I have done during the lunch hour. I thank the hon. member for giving me the opportunity to do so.
The hon. member claims that the alleged failure of a Minister of the Crown to take certain steps which he had indicated would be taken in certain circumstances is in itself a violation of Parliamentary privilege. Let me refer the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby and other hon. members, as I have done in the past, to Citation 113 of Beauchesne's fourth edition, which reads as follows:
Members often raise so-called "questions of privilege" on matters which should be dealt with as personal explanations or corrections, either in the debates or the proceedings of the House. A question of privilege ought rarely to come up in Parliament.
Do the circumstances outlined by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby give rise to a valid question of privilege? I do not think so. The circumstances alleged by the hon. member may give rise to a grievance, and grievances should normally be raised and discussed by hon. members on one of the many occasions available under our supply proceedings.
What I am suggesting to the hon. member is that although he may have a complaint and may feel that the minister has not fulfilled a promise or undertaking given to the House during the course of an answer to a question, this in itself does not, in my respectful submission, constitute a question of privilege. It is the type of grievance which should normally be taken up under other circumstances, particularly when the House is debating matters under the terms of our supply proceedings.
Neither the special privileges of the hon. member as a member of the House nor the collective privileges of the House are, to my way of thinking, at issue in this instance. I must rule, therefore, that I cannot at this time put to the House the motion proposed by the hon. member.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: BILINGUALISM AND BICULTURALISM
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL CO-OPERATION WITH PROVINCES RESPECTING PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to inform the House that this morning the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Basford) and myself have had the privilege of meeting with provincial ministers in the Ministerial Committee on Official Languages of the Constitutional Conference. During that meeting I announced to the provinces the federal government's proposals for financial co-operation in respect of bilingualism programs based on the principles set forth in Book II of the Report of the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism.
November 6, 1969

Financing of Bilingualism Programs [English']
I might add that the position we have advanced is in line with the process undertaken earlier in respect of Book I of the royal commission report, particularly the Official Languages Act which was adopted by Parliament last summer. The proposals we have advanced involve acceptance by the federal government of the principles underlying those recommendations in Book II which were addressed by the Royal Commission specifically to the federal government. They look forward to a program which would provide for federal co-operation with the provinces in greatly expanded activities in the field of minority language education and second language learning.
I am sure hon. members realize that the B and B recommendations concerning other minority groups have not yet been received.

We fully recognize that much of the substance of the recommendations of Book II of the Royal Commission Report falls more in the provincial field of responsibility than that of the federal government. At the same time, we consider that there is a national dimension to the problem. We believe that this latter aspect involves the development and encouragement of programs which will advance and encourage the use of the two official languages across the country.
Volume II of the Royal Commission Report contains 12 recommendations respecting aid to minority language schools, teacher-training, including the establishment of new teacher-training institutions; university education, including grants to minority-language students to study outside their own province, grants to minority-language universities, and a one-year transfer program for students specializing in the second official language; and finally the establishment of a Language Research Council. Other details of these programs are to be found in the statement I have made this morning.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)

Essentially, these programs would involve two related priorities; first, measures undertaken in co-operation with the provinces to ensure that the official language minorities will enjoy equal rights with the majority so far as access to education in their own language is concerned; second, the encouragement of second-language learning, to meet a desire expressed by an increasing number of

Canadians who wish to be competent in both of Canada's official languages.
As a government, we accept both these priorities and we are prepared to provide for federal financial participation in support of them. Action in this field of course calls for provincial participation as well, because proposals relating to programs and institutions in the field of education are in the provincial domain. Accordingly, in order to achieve any substantial progress in this field, provincial initiative will be required as well as a federal willingness to participate.

The question of financing is of course of the first importance. Given the financial restraints which are operative today, no government can think in terms of providing unlimited resources or establishing open-ended programs even in fields of the highest priority. We have therefore felt it necessary to inform the provinces that it will be necessary to place at least rough limits on the amounts which the federal government can contribute to this program.
Our proposals will require detailed discussion with the provincial authorities, who have of course not yet had an opportunity to study or comment on them. My purpose in speaking today is to ensure that the House is informed without delay of the government's position on this important matter. I would hope, so far as our provincial colleagues are concerned, that what we have begun this morning is a useful series of consultations which will eventually result in arrangements satisfactory to all concerned.

With the consent of the House, Mr. Speaker, I should like to table the proposals that were put to the provinces this morning which, if the House agrees, might be appended to and printed in today's Hansard.

subtopic: BILINGUALISM AND BICULTURALISM
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL CO-OPERATION WITH PROVINCES RESPECTING PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while we welcome the statement by the minister in his desire to inform Parliament, we have certain reservations and cautions about what appears to be a substantial initiative by the federal government in the field of education. Federal interference in the field of education has, in the past, been the
November 6, 1969

source of serious problems in Canada's history.
In his statement the minister recognizes that the recommendations of Book II of the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Bicul-turalism fall more in the provincial field of responsibility. But he adds that there is a federal dimension to the problem. He went on to say that the federal dimension involves the development and encouragement of programs which will advance and encourage the use of the two official languages across the country. We do not disagree with this concept. But one is too easily reminded of the development and encouragement of medicare which forced many of the provinces to swallow an unacceptable plan. Having foisted this principle on the provinces, the government is now considering removing itself from this field.
The Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) also mentioned the restraints resulting from austerity. The present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp), and ex-minister of finance, also talked of austerity as the Liberal government forced medicare on the provinces. While the federal government is limiting its contributions because of austerity, it should not push increased expenditures on the provinces. Having in mind the position in the past, I would hope that the programs proposed for federal assistance to the provinces will allow for some form of assistance not only for the two official languages but also for the other ethnic languages which have become a part of Canada's culture.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, in welcoming the statement by the minister we ask the government to exercise caution in its meetings with the provinces. Having in mind past experiences of the provinces with this government, it is probably superfluous to ask the provinces to exercise caution in dealing with the federal government.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Leader of the N.D.P.
subtopic: BILINGUALISM AND BICULTURALISM
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL CO-OPERATION WITH PROVINCES RESPECTING PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I begin my brief comments on this issue by saying immediately that so far as I am concerned I cannot see anything in the minister's statement or in the proposals which he made to the provincial ministers that suggests any intention to interfere with the provincial jurisdiction in education. I do not think one should assume this from the proposals which were made.
It has been evident from the start that if bilingualism in Canada is to be promoted and to become a reality, the major responsibility
Financing of Bilingualism Programs for it lies, in fact, with the federal government. The additional cost of enabling Canadians to learn the second official language and of increasing the teaching of the other official language in our schools should be borne by Canada as a whole through its federal treasury rather than by the provincial governments and the provincial treasuries. This is what the B and B commission indicated, and this is what we knew from the start. We therefore welcome the federal government's acceptance of that responsibility.
I have only three comments to make on the proposals that have been put before us. The first is the hope that the federal government will be as concerned with promoting the learning of other languages in Canada when the volume on other languages is produced by the B and B Commission as they have been with the promotion of the two official languages.
My second comment is that this is a field from which the federal government should never withdraw. I say this because we have had indications from the federal government of its intention to withdraw from other costsharing programs, an intention which I and my colleagues believe is contrary to the interests of Canada in those fields. But when the federal government seeks the co-operation of the provinces in introducing costly programs to promote bilingualism in Canada, the people of Canada are entitled to a firm assurance that it will not then load the provinces with the cost of that task at some future time. I do not wish to overemphasize this because although the minister did not say that in the future the government intends to withdraw from this field it is a fact that the government did not at first say it would withdraw from other cost-sharing programs, the cost of which is now being loaded entirely on the provinces. Therefore I think it is the duty of Members of Parliament to warn that any suggestion from the government of placing the burden of the cost of promoting bilingualism in Canada on the provincial treasuries would be a betrayal of the cause of bilingualism and of the obligation of this government to the people of Canada.
The third point I want to make is to express my astonishment at hearing the government pull a figure out of the air. I appreciate that any government has to allocate priorities and decide how much it can spend on A, B or C, but I am somewhat repelled by the notion that some bureaucratic group should decide that $50 million is to be spent on this project. I do not know why and how it
November 6, 1969

Financing of Bilingualism Programs decided on this amount; the minister has not told us. It seems to me it would have been much more sensible and, in my respectful submission, would have shown a great deal more good faith on the part of the federal government if it had continued discussions with the provincial governments, produced some kind of plan-or have the provinces produce plans for the promotion of bilingualism-made some kind of estimate of the cost and then related the cost to the total obligations of the federal treasury. Under such a procedure the figure might then be $35 million or $65 million or something else. But I am appalled at what I consider to be this totally bureaucratic approach of saying, without knowing what the plans are going to be, without having discussed exactly what they will be, without knowing what the cost will be: "You make plans but we place a limit of $50 million on those plans no matter what they may be." It seems to me this is not the proper approach to this kind of problem.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)
I conclude by reminding the House if I have to remind it, of my dedication to the bilingual character of this country. Therefore I cannot but greet with pleasure the federal government's involvement and its assumption of its responsibilities. I just hope that the fears I have expressed will in the future prove unjustified.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we consider it excellent policy to provide the provinces with funds for joint financing of education of minority groups of one of the official languages so that they may achieve equality with the majority group, provided the rights and powers of provinces in the field of education are respected.
I should like to remind the minister that education comes under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces, under section 93 of the British North America Act, and urge him to keep this in mind during his discussions with the provincial representatives. We trust, Mr. Speaker, that the federal government will proceed cautioustly and respect this principle, which is embodied in the Constitution.
It is obvious that on the pretense of curing a national malaise, our action should not become for the provinces another source of frustration and dissatisfaction against federalism, whatever our intentions are, if we do not comply with the terms of confederation.

Mr. Speaker, we believe that federalism must be flexible so as to respect the identify of the individual while guaranteeing its own unity and Canadian characteristic in a bicultural and bilingual atmosphere. We rejoice at the minister's statement and action, yet they leave us confused about respecting the terms of confederation.
It is utopian to imagine that all Canadians can become bilingual. However, we sincerely believe that it should be possible for anyone who wants to do so.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to conclude my remarks by saying that it is up to the federal government to help the provinces finance the program for bilingualism, show every respect for the identify and characteristics of each province, and provide for all equal opportunities to see their rights respected.
It proved more expensive for the province of Quebec to ensure the respect of bilingualism than for any other province.
Mr. Speaker, if it were possible to make such a legislation retroactive, I firmly believe that the federal government would not be in a position to repay the astronomical sums of money which the province of Quebec spent to maintain federalism, while in other provinces unilingualism was promoted. If every province will extend to its minority the same respect which the province of Quebec has shown to its minority, we of the Ralliement creditiste believe that national unity is possible.
That is why we are pleased with the initiative of the federal government, provided naturally that it will respect the identity and the jurisdiction of each of the provinces.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising on a point of order. At this stage I must, with great respect, challenge the right of this House, pursuant to Standing Order No. 70, to receive this bill. I should like Your Honour's leave to put the circumstances before the House very briefly, without in any sense opposing the principle of the bill or what is involved in it.
In all seriousness I suggest to Your Honour that an attempt to place the bill before the House in this way constitutes a violation of the British North America Act, and in addition violates two of our most important standing Orders, Nos. 62 and 63. I should like to read to you the clause in the bill which I submit makes it repugnant as far as this House is concerned:
3(2). The provisions made by any Appropriation Act to defray the expenses of the board shall be applied to such classifications of the public service within the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources as the Governor in Council may determine.
It is my submission that this is in fact an appropriation within the meaning of our rules and within the meaning of the British North America Act as well as within our traditions and practices. I need hardly remind Your Honour that the British North America Act, particularly clauses 53 and 54, states:
53.	Bills for appropriating any Part of the Public Revenue, or for imposing any Tax or Impost, shall originate in the House of Commons.
54.	It shall not be lawful for the House of Commons to adopt or pass any Vote, Resolution, Address, or Bill for the Appropriation of any Part of the Public Revenue, or of any Tax or Impost, to any Purpose that has not been first recommended to that House by Message of the Governor Genera] in the Session in which such Vote, Resolution, Address, or Bill is proposed.
Standing Order 62 provides:
1. This House shall not adopt or pass any vote, resolution, address or bill for the appropriation of any part of the public revenue, or of any tax or impost, to any purpose that has not been first recommended to the House by a message from the Governor General in the session in which such vote, resolution, address or bill is proposed.

Dominion Coal Board Dissolution Act
Then, Mr. Speaker, pursuant to the changes in Standing Orders which were made last year there is provision that:
2. The message and recommendation of the Governor General in relation to any bill for the appropriation of any part of the public revenue or of any tax or impost shall be printed on the Notice Paper and in the Votes and Proceedings when any such measure is to be introduced and the text of such recommendation shall be printed with or annexed to every such bill.
I cannot answer for what message may or may not have been sent by His Excellency, but certainly none has been printed in Votes and Proceedings. I would point out to Your Honour that there has been a breach of what from the time of antiquity has been one of the rights and privileges of this House, to vote and appropriate money for a specific purpose which this House may see fit to direct to that end. Beyond any question, clauses 2 and 3 of Bill S-3 deal with an appropriation of moneys for a specific purpose not covered by a Commons appropriation bill of this session.
[DOT] (2:30 p.m.)
The purpose of this bill has been initiated in the other place. Large sums of money may or may not be involved; all I can say is that an examination of the Appropriation Acts will reveal that for the current fiscal year the sum of $180,000 has been set apart for the purpose of meeting the expenses of administration of the Dominion Coal Board which is being dissolved by Bill S-3. In addition, there appears in an appropriation bill of 1964 a certain sum which was added to in 1966. The total provision is for a sum of $22 million to be expended over a five-year period on matters coming under the jurisdiction of the Coai Board.
That, simply, is my reason for objecting to this bill. It constitutes an appropriation of funds for a purpose which this House has not necessarily approved and which has not been recommended in a message from His Excellency. In other words, the spending of the unexpended funds referred to in the bill ought not to be applied to the classification of the Public Service as the Governor in Council may determine by clause 3(2).
It may well be that if this bill were allowed to proceed and subjected to the normal proceedings of this House, it would be competent for the government at any time to initiate in the other place a bill to set aside certain payments and programs covered by measures or statutes properly recommended by His
November 6, 1969

Inquiries of the Ministry Excellency and divert the money for other purposes. I am of course referring to purposes for which money has been appropriated. True, the matter would have to come back to this House for discussion, but I submit most sincerely that if that were done there would be a flouting of the provisions of the Standing Orders of this House and of the constitution.
I conclude by saying that in the past 18 months the power of the government has expanded far too much and the power of the Commons has been eroded in a studied fashion. I submit, therefore, that we cannot permit this bill to go through unchallenged. That is why I have raised this issue. Your Honour may wish to take the matter under advisement and bring down a decision on whether the bill ought to be allowed to proceed.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, November 5, consideration of the motion of Mr. Pepin that Bill C-6, to wind up the Canadian Corporation for the 1967 World Exhibition and to authorize the writing-off of certain costs and the deferral of certain payments connected therewith, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

subtopic: CANADIAN WORLD EXHIBITION CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before coming to the heart of the matter, I should like to request your indulgence since, for a few seconds, I shall be in order only partly, I think; in this case, I base myself on a precedent created yesterday, for I heard some of my colleagues pay tribute to those who were at the origin of the Canadian Corporation for the World Exhibition. For instance, they referred to the honourable Mark Drouin, who has died since, and to the Commissioner, His Excellency Pierre Dupuy, who served with such distinction and who has also left us for a better world.
I feel I am complying with the wishes of every hon. member in paying tribute also to a great man, one who has contributed the most to the creation of Expo, that is Mr. Jean Drapeau, mayor of Montreal. I am doing it not only because I believe he deserves the gratefulness of all hon. members and of all Canadians but also the sympathy of the house and of every Canadian for the shocking, ungrateful and dirty way he has been treated since then by people throwing bombs at his house and his place of business.
Having said this, I now turn to Bill C-6 entitled: An Act to wind up the Canadian Corporation for the 1967 World Exhibition and to authorize the writing-off of certain costs and the deferral of certain payments
November 6, 1989

connected therewith. The explanatory note states clearly that the purposes of this bill is:
(a)	to provide for the dissolution of the Canadian Corporation for the 1967 World Exhibition;
Nobody can object to that, I think, because it is in order.
The second purpose of this bill is, and I quote:
(b)	to authorize the disposition of the remaining assets and liabilities of the Corporation;
There might be differences of opinion as to the manner of disposing of the assets and liabilities, but the government proposes a solution which will be discussed at the meetings of the appropriate committee. The third purpose of this bill is:
(c)	to stop interest accruing on the outstanding notes of the Corporation payable to the Government of Canada and thus prevent the accumulation of additional liability in respect of those notes and to write-off one hundred and twenty-five million dollars representing Canada's share of the deficit of the Corporation;
It must be admitted that this is an economy measure which can be easily accounted for and it will be possible to put questions to the minister in the committee.
Here is the fourth purpose of the bill:
(d)	to authorize the deferral to 1972 of payment by Quebec of not more than five million five hundred thousand dollars due in 1969-70 in connection with the operations of the Corporation.
As we know, the government has taken such action in order to take advantage of the request made by the city of Montreal to cope with unemployment there. It is therefore a rather fictitious expenditure, since the equivalent would have been spent on unemployment insurance and welfare allowances.
The minister explained in greater detail the reasons for every provision of the bill.
After the minister's statement, the bill seemed quite clear and simple to me, and even the opposition praised it no end. Therefore, I thought the debate would only take a few hours, just long enough perhaps to hear the few usual speeches from members of the opposition, so that the measure could be referred to the appropriate parliamentary committee, where questions and explanations could be asked, concern expressed and answers obtained from the minister and his experts.
I would not have dared intervene in the debate if all members had agreed that it might save time. But since the whole day yesterday was spent in bringing all kinds of
Dissolution of Expo 1967 Corporation charges against the government and distorting the facts, I feel duty bound today to answer at least briefly.
While I felt the debate was unnecessary, I listened to all the interventions of the opposition, including statements that were petty and at times disquieting.
I hope that I am mistaken, because I do not pride myself on being infallible. However, I thought I perceived in certain members an intention to express, indirectly and discreetly, while heaping praises on the minister, some feelings of jealousy toward the city of Montreal and the province of Quebec because of Expo. Some also took the opportunity to attack the government.
Mr. Speaker, in my view this is uncalled for,, since we are dealing with an exceptional measure. In fact "Man and his World" has been the finest monument ever erected to the Canadian way of life, for all the world to see, thanks to the co-operation of all-whoever they may be: the Progressive Conservative party, other parties or all citizens, even those who are not interested in politics.
This achievement was the result of co-operation from the beginning. At least this time we managed to agree on a tremendous achievement for the sake of Canada's prestige. I think we should not give the rest of the world the impression we are mice trying to nibble away at this monument's base, but that we can work together and complete this wonderful undertaking that was launched so successfully.
Of course, some people always worry and we must try to reassure them.
First of all, I wish to deny that this was a gift to the city of Montreal, and I can prove it. On the contrary, I believe, as I already said, that it was a co-operative effort from all Canadians toward the development of this country, and that Montrealers and Quebecers did more than their share, or at least their share, shall we say, not to exaggerate.
We are told that Expo cost every Canadian $7, but it is perhaps not known that it also cost Quebecers more than $7. They have indeed paid $18, Montrealers have paid $75, not taking into account the sharing of the deficit that we shall pay as Canadians, Quebecers and Montrealers. The contribution of each Montrealer, Mr. Speaker, will amount to some $75.
This is to say that Quebecers, mostly Montrealers, have done more than their share and have not really got anything free, gratis and
November 6, 1969

Dissolution of Expo 1967 Corporation for nothing. Rather it is they who gave something to the rest of the country in their great kindness, a present so to speak, but I shall not stress that word unduly. At least they proved their willingness to do their share.
The same holds true for the breakdown of Expo costs: they said that Canada would finance 50 per cent of the cost, Quebec 37| per cent and Montreal 12 per cent. However, with respect to the 50 per cent contributed by the federal government, we must recognize that about 16 per cent thereof comes from taxes collected in the province of Quebec. Therefore, Quebec did its share.
I have quoted those figures for the benefit of those who might worry and who think that on this occasion there was a lack of distributive justice in Canada; I would like to show them that, on the contrary, Quebecers and mostly Montrealers are willing to co-operate with the rest of the country, when Canada's welfare is at stake.
In the course of this debate, Mr Speaker, it has also been said to my amazement that Expo cost considerably more than had been anticipated originally. I have here the official report of the House of Commons debates recording the words of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) in this matter. Indeed on December 20, 1963, as is recorded at page 6213, the latter spoke in the following terms and I quote:

In 1959 the Montreal chamber of commerce prepared a brief. In 1960, on February 10, I announced that Canada would apply to I.B.E. for the fair; that Ottawa would guarantee $20 million, Quebec $15 million and the city of Montreal $5 million.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)

That is what had been anticipated in 1960.
Mr. Speaker, I feel almost tempted to be nasty to my friends opposite and remind them that the then responsible authorities for Expo, the Commissioner at that time, were of the same politicial stripe as they are. I have the feeling that those people-his associates and himself-lacked vision, did not imagine that Canada had to meet a greater challenge than what they pictured.
Those figures, moreover, were much too conservative. They did not show enough vision to anticipate the great support from people all over the world who would come to Canada on that occasion, to anticipate the number of countries which would wish to take part in Expo, as well as the number of

statesmen who would come here with impressive retinues to visit what Canada and all the other participating countries had to show to the modern world.
I forgive them for making wrong predictions, but the government should not now be blamed for shortsightedness because the people who made wrong predictions had been appointed by our friends on the other side.
Mr. Speaker, I readily admit that nobody in the world could have forecast in 1960, 1961, 1962 or 1963 the tremendous success of the exhibition. Planning was as sound as could be but, considering the unprecedented number of countries anxious to take part in Expo and the millions of people who were then planning to visit us, the Expo site had to be enlarged, facilities and staff had to be increased. They were recruited within the private sector and, since it was for temporary employment, they obviously had to be paid more than had been expected.
Mr. Speaker, it is no cause for surprise that the exhibition should have left us with a deficit of $143 million, at least as far as the federal government is concerned. No matter what the Auditor General says, I maintain that the exhibition has left us with assets worth more than that deficit. The Auditor General of Canada has overlooked them. They are most valuable and more than compensate the deficit for Canada.
These are moral assets, Mr. Speaker: invaluable prestige, such as Canada never enjoyed before and acquired through the exhibition which brought citizens of many other countries to visit us. They now know the true image of Canada, a giant emerging from sleep in 1969, thanks, first of all, to Expo, then to "Man and His World."
Mr. Speaker, such things are bought and are paid for, even with money, nowadays. The research and the experiments that were carried out will bear fruit in many sectors of our economy and of our industry. What nobody would have dared undertake before because the necessary money could not be found in the usual budgets, was done with the Expo budget. Such things will profit our scientists, manufacturers and businessmen for centuries. All year round, funds are being spent for research and our friends opposite are the first to blame the government for not investing enough in that field. Now, we had a unique opportunity for research which resulted some new techniques.
Mr. Speaker, the federal government's share in the deficit have contributed to the
November 6. 1969	COMMONS
advancement of research. The results were so many that I would have to speak for hours on end to explain what I have seen, and I am only a layman.
What about the publicity given to Canada and its undertakings? Everyone knows how publicity is costly. My friends opposite are the first to criticize the government sometimes for spending too much on publicity for Canada. We got the benefit of indirect publicity which would have cost us millions of dollars and would not have been as effective, since it attracted to Canada a great number of visitors who came to see for themselves that our country was one of the most active in the world.
With regard to the Expo deficit, we should keep in mind the Auditor General's function.
I do not want to criticize him because his job is not to appraise moral, intellectual or scientific values but to add figures. He is doing a fine job. If reliance is placed solely on his evidence to condemn the deficit of Expo '67, then any argument is unfair and practically dishonest in some cases.
What has Expo brought us that does not appear in the official reports? Revenue in the form of taxes that have been derived from the tourist trade. This means considerable sums of money that have not been added to the good results brought about by Expo. Today, when this great event has ended brilliantly, some would start beefing-if I may use this expression that is not taken from Bossu-et-when we have succeeded in building something as tremendous as that, without taking into account a number of things that undeniably and unquestionably exist and that have brought to Canada considerable and needed additional revenue for the benefit of all Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, Expo '67 has brought us more than that still. I am thinking of the ties which have been established through Expo. A number of businessmen came from various countries to establish commercial and industrial connections with Canadian businessmen, financiers and manufacturers. Such connections are of priceless value to the Canadian people. Let us think of that, rather than criticize additional expenses which by the way, are nothing out of the ordinary, since the initial estimates go back to 1960 and the scope of this exhibition has more than doubled; actually it increased fourfold, as compared with the first estimations.
Mr. Speaker, Expo had another result that adding machines will not be able to compute:
DEBATES	595
Dissolution of Expo 1967 Corporation it reinforced national unity. All the countries which took part in the World Exhibition and whose citizens came to Canada, join hands today in a spirit of good will; they have gained a better mutual understanding and have a sincere desire for peace.
Those results of Expo cannot be denied. I believe the deficit of Expo, which will cost Canadians $125 million, not to mention the City of Montreal and the province of Quebec, will be offset by the circulation of additional money.
Expo will have tangible results. As I said before, Expo is the most beautiful memorial ever erected to Canadianism. All Canadians should rally around this memorial, and give up all petty thoughts at this point, when Expo is about to wind up.
Mr. Speaker, I think that I should bring my comments to a close, even if it is only to prove that I believe a little in what I have just said.
What is the minister asking us to do, after having given his explanations? To refer that bill to the parliamentary committee, because he will be there with his experts and he will answer all our questions. If we are not satisfied, the bill will be sent back to the House and we will then be free to air our grievances.
The opposition has the right to question public expenditures, but at least when an important achievement which will affect the future of Canada and of many other countries is concerned, hon. members should certainly not make malicious assumptions or dubious statements.
In my view-and all government members agree with me, I think-one must admit, so that no doubts remain in the minds of the members of the opposition, that Expo was an achievement to which everyone contributed to the full extent of their power, even the opposition parties.
As good citizens of Canada, we should put an end to all objections and hasten to refer this bill to the designated committee where questions can be asked and answers listened to and checked, so that the bill may come back to the House where every member will be able to vote on it according to his lights.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is where we pay up for our one-hundredth birthday party and I believe
November 6, 1969

Dissolution of Expo 196 7 Corporation most Canadians are willing to pay if convinced the overspending was reasonable. I believe there is very little disposition in the minds of Canadians generally to question cases of additional expenditure where reasonable overtime was required and where things were done in good faith to make the birthday party and Expo a success. However, I rather resent some of the remarks of the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain). I should like to answer in a friendly spirit, and perhaps explain to him some of the things which motivate those of us who are questioning the expenditures for Expo.
I do not think we can ignore any instances of bad faith there may have been during the construction of the Expo site, nor can we afford to make further mistakes in winding up the Expo corporation.
I should like to make some comments on the hon. member's speech, Mr. Speaker. He seemed to think there might be some hidden jealousy of Montreal in the speeches of members of the opposition and suggested that where good projects were involved, troublesome minds were at work. But, Mr. Speaker, I do not think there is anybody in this country who feels any resentment toward either Montreal or Quebec in connection with Expo 67. As a matter of fact, it is exactly the opposite; it was a tremendous national project in which Montreal, the Province of Quebec and all Canadians joined. We were proud of Montreal, of the show they put on, and we were proud of the people of the province of Quebec. People from all over the country went to Montreal for Expo 67, were thrilled by it and heartened by the friendliness of the people of Quebec. They returned to their homes full of good will. Surely, no one is trying to spoil this result of a real effort on the part of all Canadians.
However, government supervision of the project and the activities in connection with winding it up must be questioned. At least, these are matters which concern me. There is no doubt in the world that a lot of mistakes were made as a result of bad judgment, and these cost money. I am sure some can be justified by the fact that there was a time limit; there was just no way of postponing the day of opening. However, we do not have this excuse now and further mistakes in winding up should be prevented, although there are some things in this bill which I believe to be wrong.
The hon. member for Trois-Rivieres said that all Canadians had benefltted financially

from Expo 67. In a sense that is true, but I come from a tourist area in a tourist province and I can tell the hon. member that in my riding of Parry Sound-Muskoka, and in Ontario generally, tourist revenues in 1967 dropped as low as they have ever been. They dropped right down to nothing because everybody was going to Montreal. However, I never heard one word of complaint. People felt that if they were losing money, then they would probably make up for it the next year. The deficit about which we are talking amounts to $7 per head, but some of these people lost thousands. They just hoped that then- usual customers would return the next year. The hope had been expressed that tourists would take a triangular or circular tour through our part of the country when returning to their homes in the United States or the west. This did not happen but people in my riding did not complain about it. This is the spirit in which the great effort of the city of Montreal was accepted. Nevertheless, it must not be forgotten that they did lose large sums of money.
The hon. member for Trois-Rivieres also mentioned generosity, and asked if we were going to be niggardly about a few million dollars in settling the affairs of this Corporation. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) pointed out that Winnipeg has a deficit of less than one million dollars as a result of the Pan-Am Games, a pittance compared with Expo. However, as far as I can gather, this government has not made any commitment to assist in this regard.

Mr. Speaker, I have very few comments to make, following which I hope the minister will be able to answer the questions which have been asked.
I want to join with the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) in denying categorically that, as far as I am concerned, there is any question of jealousy or of being upset in the context of the remarks of the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain). All Canadians were proud of the fact that Expo was held in the way it was; that it was held in the city of Montreal, in the province of Quebec; that it brought to Canadians all over the country a sense of exhilaration, joy and happiness. It was a great event, and no one I know of has ever suggested anything to the contrary.
But, Mr. Speaker, it is over, finished. The money has been spent. I think we agree with the Tentmaker, who said:
The Moving Finger writes; and, having writ,
Moves on; nor all your Piety nor Wit
Shall lure it back to cancel half a Line,
Nor all your Tears wash out a Word of it.
Although we cannot now do anything about money that has been spent, I am here as one of 264 trustees of the people of Canada whose money is being utilized in a variety of ways. Consequently, I would be derelict in the exercise of my duty were I not to call to the attention of the House, and I hope ultimately to the committee, certain facts in connection with the financial program and administration of this Corporation.
I would not call back one cent, one five cent piece, of the money that was needed to be spent on the great and glorious spectacle that was Expo. Neither do I know of any member on this side of the House who would want to call back any of that money. However, I come from an area where there are a million acres under the snow; where thousands of people will have extreme difficulty in eking out a living this year; where, as the minister knows, there are tens of millions of bushels of grain which will not be harvested until next spring, and probably not harvested successfully even then.

DEBATES	November 6, 1969
I would not be carrying out my responsibility if I did not challenge certain of the workings of this Corporation with regard to Expo. I conceive it my duty to call to account people, corporations and administrations which have been delinquent, which have been guilty of extravagance and waste.
As to the future, we do not know what other areas of expenditure may be taken in hand. The lessons of Expo may well be lessons that can be usefully exploited and utilized by this or succeeding governments that undertake responsibilities that are related in their nature to the undertaking that was Expo.
With this in mind, Mr. Speaker, just what do we find? Right from the inception of this Corporation, an officer of this Parliament, independent and answerable only to Parliament, saw fit, in the exercise of his duties, to call to our attention, through the medium of the successive reports published by him, a number of aspects concerning the administration of Expo which he, the Auditor General, considered very dubious and which, at the very least, required explanation. These observations appear in the 1964 report and are pursued in the reports of 1965, 1966, 1967 and 1968. I am quite convinced that the report for the fiscal year ending March 1969 will also have some interesting observations to make on this subject.
Merely because we say that Expo was a good show, a good party, that the people of Montreal and their mayor, the people of the province of Quebec, indeed the people of Canada, did a good job in putting it on, does not absolve us from the responsibility of making a careful examination of these accounts. All we can do, of course, is to carry on a post-mortem, and in this respect I wish to bring certain matters briefly to the attention of the House. Then, I will make a suggestion.
For example, may I refer to a matter that was brought to my attention by a person in my constituency, a constituency in which, as a result of certain factors, people occasionally read the report of the Auditor General. At page 154 of the Auditor General's report for the fiscal year 1966-67 appears this paragraph:
In several cases relocation expenses involving substantial moving hotel and living expenses of newly-appointed senior officers and employees over extended periods would not have qualified for payment under the regulations laid down by the federal or provincial Treasury Boards. From the inception of the Corporation to December 31, 1966, approximately $150,000 has been spent on removal

Let me refer to some of the questions of a general nature which should be answered. I have just given illustrations of the more exorbitant and flagrant type of thing that has happened. We are entitled to have information about the investigation in respect of salary rates and termination payments. I suggest nothing would be lost if this were done. The standing committee to which the bill will be referred will be engaged in many other matters. I know it will want to deal with certain aspects of the bill itself. The Public Accounts Committee is set up to handle studies of this kind. It should look into this whole situation with the Auditor General and his officials in attendance. They should delve into the questions asked by members of this and other parties in the opposition. These questions should be answered before the winding up is completed.
When this bill is passed the corporation will have been wound up and will be functus officio. It is my respectful submission that it should not be wound up until adequate answers have been supplied. I, therefore, urge the minister who will be replying shortly to give very careful consideration to this suggestion. A lot of questions have been asked. I might feel sorry for the minister were it not for the fact he has escaped from the problems of the Wheat Board and is now faced with the problems of Expo which are, I believe, the lesser of two evils. Surely, he is willing, on behalf of the government and the people of

I shall say a few words only to point out that during yesterday's and today's discussions we totally agreed on at least two points: first of all, on Expo's considerable success. I had brought a refrigerator almost full of famous quotations from Canadians and foreigners concerning Expo '67. It will not be necessary for me to use them, since hon. members have proved themselves equal to the occasion to point out this great success.
However, I am taking the liberty of reminding the house that usually such a success is relatively expensive in terms of human efforts and money. For a sum of $20 million, you can have what you pay for: a small circus, a regional exhibition. However, to get an international and universal exhibition, you must pay the price. In fact, I was reading in a newspaper, a few days ago, that the Japanese expect their exhibition to cost them $2,300,000,000. It would thus have been rather odd if Canada had been able to manage with only a dozen millions or two. In other words, to have an exhibition which will not be a disappointment, you have to pay the price.
Secondly, total agreement was reached on the advisability of obtaining from the committee the answers to the questions which have been raised and while I rose two or three times to interrupt the speeches of my hon. friends, it was not to deny them the right to direct questions; it was to try and shorten the debate because some of them proved inclined to draw conclusions based on false premises. maintopic: CHILDREN OF WAR DEAD (EDUCATION ASSISTANCE) ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY, ETC.
speechtext:
that Bill C-8, to amend the Children of War Dead (Education Assistance) Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs.
He said:

-Mr. Speaker, the bill now before the House deals with a legislative measure which has been in existence for sixteen years, more precisely since April 13, 1953. At that date, the legislation was received with enthusiasm by all members of all parties. The Children of War Dead (Education Assistance) Act is based upon two principles closely related: firstly, to allow those young people to complete their
November 6, 1969

Children of War Dead Act education and, secondly, to recognize the special obligation of the state towards the children of Canadian war dead who gave their lives for their country.
Mr. Speaker, I think Canadians can rightly be proud of this legislation. Since it came into effect, many young people who benefited from its provisions later on expressed their gratitude to the Minister and to the Department. Thus, I received a few weeks ago a letter of which I would like to quote an excerpt:
The bill with respect of children of War dead is an excellent legislation; my daughter Linda feels as I do that It is a distinguished tribute to the memory of her father.
Mr. Speaker, the number of recipients clearly indicates that the law is attaining its true objective. Since its enforcement on July 1, 1953, 4,801 orphans of soldiers, veterans or certain special classes of civilians have been in a position to carry on post-secondary studies. Of that number, 2,201 successfully completed their studies, 135 of them during the financial year 1968-1969. In the course of that same year, 330 students were enabled to start their studies through assistance provided under the Act, i.e. 16 more than in the previous year. On March 31, 1969, 899 students were pursuing their studies under this plan throughout Canada.
Mr. Speaker, since 1953, the Act has been amended four times, to make its benefits available to groups of children not covered by the initial Act, to increase the amounts applicable to tuition and other related expenses, and also to increase the amounts of monthly allowances and, in certain special cases, to extend the period over which allowances are payable beyond the 36 months or 4 academic years initially provided.
From 1953 to 1963, beneficiaries included primarily students whose father or mother died or were killed during World War II. During the last six years, they included mostly children of veterans killed in Korea, of deceased members of the regular forces or of deceased World War II pensioners.
All members will agree I am sure, that that piece of legislation has been most useful, not only to those who are directly concerned, but to the general public.
Mr. Speaker, I now wish to ask the house to approve two amendments that not only will eliminate certain anomalies but will also give full justice to the students to whom the act applies.

First of all, we want to extend the application of this measure to a group of children, approximately 80 in number at the present time, who receive a pension under section 25 of the Pension Act. As many members know, according to section 25 of the Pension Act, the Canadian Pension Commission is authorized to pay a compassionate pension, an allocation or a supplementary pension in certain worthy cases where the claimant is not otherwise entitled to a pension.
Section 25 is therefore very useful where technical considerations make it impossible to grant a pension in the usual way, that is because of statutory entitlement. For instance, when a veteran dies before the Canadian Pension Commission has been able to decide on the question of eligibility or to assess disability which existed before death, section 25 allows the granting of a pension to his children. Section 25 allows in fact the Commission to conclude from the medical file that it would have declared itself in favour of eligibility had the veteran lived.
Mr. Speaker, I guess it is not the appropriate moment to discuss the technical details of the Pension Act. In fact I was only mentioning a case relating to the first of the two suggested amendments.
I should like to add that the suggested amendment derives from a recommendation of the Woods Commission which suggested that, when a pension is granted on compassionate grounds to a widow, her children who are entitled to pension should be eligible to the educational allowances provided by the Education Assistance Act. Moreover, with this amendment, the children of a widow who does not benefit from a pension, or does not live with them, would be eligible to this assistance.
Mr. Speaker, the second amendment that we shall have to study pertains to section 7 of the Pension Act. It concerns students who fail their examinations and to whom is given the right to try a second examination. At the present time, any student who fails more than one supplementary examination is deprived of any other assistance provided for in section 7. This exclusion results from the standard of success that used to be imposed to student veterans, at the end of World War II. It was in accordance with requirements from colleges, universities and other educational institutions, at the time this legislation was enacted. As a rule, the students were required to give up their studies under the circumstances I have just mentioned. However, these educational institutions, colleges and universities
November 6, 1969	COMMONS
have modified their rules in the last few years, thus creating abnormalities resulting in unfair treatment.
Let us take the ease of two students in the same university or faculty who failed their examinations: one of them failed for lack of a few marks only, while the other one failed by a wider margin. Perhaps the university will offer the first one the privilege of trying supplementary examinations and should he fail several of them, he might be authorized to repeat his year and then proceed normally with his studies. However, he would not be entitled to any financial aid because section 7 forbids subsidizing students who have failed more than one supplementary examination. The second student mentioned, who was barred from the supplementary examination because of lower marks and a poorer general standing, can repeat his year and get his degree. However, under the present legislation, the latter who has failed to a greater extent than the former can obtain financial aid after successful completion of the year that he failed.
Another oddity occurs when two students attending the exact same courses in two different universities fail their examinations. One of those institutions offers supplementary examinations and section 7 of the Act then applies to that student. The other university does not offer supplementary examinations so that the student attending the latter university is not liable to the exclusion provided for by the said section. Those two examples point to an obvious injustice, and we hope these amendments will correct the situation.
I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, that hon. members recognize the benefits of the Children of War Dead (Education Assistance) Act. Also, I am positive that all members want this Act to be brought in line with current practices being followed in Canadian educational institutions and eligible students to get approximately what their parents would have given them had they lived.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to comment briefly on the minister's statement which I think was an excellent one. It covered this bill very well. The Children of War Dead (Education Assistance), Act, which was introduced in 1953, is perhaps the finest piece of legislation in the entire veterans' charter. In 1946, at the very first national convention of the Canadian 21362-39
DEBATES	605
Children of War Dead Act Legion held following the end of World War II, and which I attended, this matter was discussed. It was again pressed in 1948, 1950 and 1952, and in 1953 the federal government enacted the legislation, mainly in the form in which we presently find it.
One unfortunate thing about the enactment of the legislation was that it was a full eight years after the end of World War II before it became effective. As a result we had examples of older men, perhaps not older in relation to many of us now, who had children getting out of high school in 1945 and 1946, and of other men who were killed, or who died of war wounds and who left children still attending high school. These children were not able to benefit from the act. After the act became effective in 1953 the children of war dead, and of those who subsequently died from their wounds, were protected under the act.
I was interested to hear the minister's figures showing that 4,800 students have benefited under the act, and that over 2,000 students have completed their education. He also pointed out that roughly 900 are presently in schools or attending university. This also includes students attending nursing schools.
The minister's explanation of the clauses in the bill was helpful, but through you, Mr. Speaker, I say to him that it must be in the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs that this legislation is thoroughly examined, with the assistance of very able departmental officials, especially from the Welfare Department, who will answer our questions. At first reading, clause 2 in particular, amending section 7 of the act, looks highly technical. I have had some discussion with officials of the Department of Veterans Affairs on the bill and as a result I understand exactly what is proposed. However, I am sure many other hon. members would find it difficult to follow.
I can assure hon. members that everything proposed in this bill is good. I only wish we had been able to amend the Act a few years earlier, but for the delay the present minister cannot be held responsible in any way. As I say, the amendments in this bill are excellent.
I was interested to note that the minister pointed out that this is one of the first of the Woods Commission recommendations to come before Parliament in the form of legislation. It is only fitting that our finest piece of veterans' legislation should be the first to be amended. I conclude by saying I feel the members of this party-I cannot speak for all the others, only for myself-the members of

GRANTS TO INDIAN BAND COUNCILS Mr. Frank Howard (Skeena) moved:
That an Order of the House do issue for a copy of any document prepared in the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development entitled, or relating to "Grants to Indian Band Councils" subsequent to the issuance of Circular No. 15, dated September 18, 1968, which is entitled "Grants to Indian Band Councils."
He said: Mr. Speaker, there is a short history relating to the particular document for which production is sought, a short history that I think shows an element of refusal on the part of the government to be totally and completely honest with the general public, and to be open in so far as its activities are concerned with our native Indian people. There has been a confined, narrow, bureaucratic and legislatively fine concept which has permitted the present difficulties to arise. 
In referring to this matter, I must go back to May 28 of this year in the preceding session when a motion, identical in wording, was presented to the House. As recorded at page 9163 of Hansard for that date a response was given by the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Forest) as follows:
On behalf of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development I would like to inform the hon. member that subsequent to the issuance of circular 15, dated September 18,	1968, entitled
"Grants to Indian Band Councils", no additional documents have been issued.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
Under the circumstances would the hon. member from Skeena consent to withdrawing the motion?
I did not so consent, but had the motion transferred for debate. The opportunity to debate it did not arise but I think it is important, apropos of what I said earlier about a deliberate refusal to be completely open with the public about these matters, to point out that the motion made on the 28th of May for the production of that document asked for the production of any document prepared in the department relating to that subject. I think it is important to notice that the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Forest) who has a particularly esteemed and high position within the government, deliberately phrased his response to avoid making reference to the request in the motion for any document that was prepared, but simply talked about any documents that were issued.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, this sort of legalistic nit-picking was deliberately designed to confuse the issue and cover up something within the department. Otherwise, why did the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council ignore the particular request in the motion for any document that was "prepared" and use instead the word "issued", to which no reference was made.
Here, we have exactly the same motion, exactly the same words, but now we have a newly appointed Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Honey). As an aside, I am sure Your Honour will not mind if I wish him well in his appointment. Presumably, if he works well and carefully, he may rise to higher and greater things within the structure of government. I shall be quite happy to cooperate with him in any way in the performance of his duties, but I would probably cause him some difficulties. However, that is

the way things happen. In any event, yesterday the Parliamentary Secretary, in response to the motion which I put to the House, said:
Mr. Speaker, the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has no record of any document prepared-
And here the word "prepared" is used. I think this is the correct approach because that is what I am seeking to obtain, any document prepared by the department. He says the department "has no record of any document prepared subsequent to the issuance of Circular No. 15 dated September 18, 1968" relating to certain matters.
I would not say this unless I were fairly sure of my ground and I do not mean it unkindly, but knowing how things work within the government, I think it is probable that some one in the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development prepares a reply to a motion. The reply is then handed to the unsuspecting minister or parliamentary secretary for presentation to the House. So when the parliamentary secretary stated yesterday that the "Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has no record of any document prepared subsequent to the issuance of Circular No. 15" relating to the subject matter contained therein, I think this is a deliberate attempt to maintain an element of secrecy and keep information from the public. It is a deliberate and conscious effort to deny to the Indian people access to a document prepared by the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development which relates to grants to Indian Band Councils. The government seems content to present to the public, by way of press release, only those things it wants to present and to keep hidden those things it wants to hide. It is more intent upon propagandizing than upon public disclosure.
I cite this development as a preliminary to the argument for the production of this particular document or any document because, as I said earlier, regardless of what the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council said on the 28th May and regardless of what the parliamentary secretary said yesterday about there being no record of any such document, there is in fact a document which can easily be identified and was identified by the motion before us. The identification of the document in the motion before us was extracted from the document in question. Lest there be any doubt, I have in my hand this document which does not exist, of which the Department of Indian Affairs 21362-39^

and Northern Development has no record; this document which the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council skirted around on May 28th.
The document is on a piece of paper which has right at the top, in the English language so that it is properly identified, "Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development", the very department about which we are talking. The French version is underneath that. There is the coat of arms with "Canada" underneath it and a place along the right hand side for the file number or "dossier". If the massive and highly efficient Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has no record of such a document, I would be quite happy to make mine available so that they would have a record of it. This is a simple, ordinary document from the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, prepared within that department, distributed to every Indian agency in Canada, distributed to quite a number of chiefs of Indian Band Councils, and distributed to regional directors within the Indian Affairs Branch.

The hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) has been very congenial in his remarks but has been somewhat critical of departmental officials. I think perhaps he may have overstated the case. I ask him to read again the notices of motion prepared for the previous session of parliament and for the present session of parliament. Does he think that the officials of the department or anyone else, for that matter, could reasonably identify from the wording of the motions the particular document he has in mind? I have been able to identify the document after listening to the hon. member's remarks this afternoon. I suspect, however, that without his assistance in this debate it would have been quite difficult or almost impossible to sort out his

document from the several hundred memoranda which each year emanate from the department to regional directors, chiefs of Indian bands, and so on, on the question of consultation between the minister and his officials and the Indians of Canada. If I have correctly identified the document, it is only because the hon. member has been of assistance this afternoon. It would have been very difficult to identify it from his notice of motion.
I think the document we are speaking about is the memorandum that was prepared to be circulated to regional directors of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, chiefs of Indian band councils and superintendents of Indian agencies, with a view to obtaining the views of the Indians of Canada, through their bands and in consultation and discussion with officials of the department, on certain modifications that were proposed with respect to grants to Indian band councils. A cursory reading of the document will reveal that it was not intended to be a final document. Its purpose was only to provide a basis of consultation with the Indian peoples. I think it might be helpful if I were to note two or three items in the covering letter which accompanied this particular memorandum to regional directors and to others to whom it was circulated. This letter is from the then director of the department, Mr. David A. Munro, and I wish to quote two or three extracts from this letter. Mr. Munro said in part:
You will recall that the Grants to Bands Program was discussed during the Regional Directors' Conference last December. I indicated to you that as soon as modifications to the existing program as requested by the Indian people could be embodied in the new proposal it would be referred to you to ensure that the Indians in your Region would be given the opportunity to give us their views on the modified formula.
The letter goes on to say:
There are herewith ...
A proposal on the Grants to Bands Program, embodying certain changes intended to meet the wishes of Indians to be used by you-
Meaning, by the Regional Director. I continue:
-as a basis for discussion with them.
Copies of Blue Circulars 4, 9, 13 and 15, which will be rescinded and replaced by a new circular after an agreement has been reached on the modified program.
It is apparent from the covering letter and the document itself that this was only the basis of consultation. There was to be a reporting back to the minister and his officials

in Ottawa, and the reactions of Indians throughout Canada would be considered. Then the minister, in consultation with his officials, would decide whether the particular modifications could be adopted on the basis of reports received from the Indian peoples of Canada. The last paragraph of the letter which, 1 repeat, was sent to regional directors across the country, reads:
Would you, therefore, by February 21st, please supply me with a statement of the reaction of Indians to the proposals contained in the draft circular attached, together with a clear statement of the manner in which you have consulted with them.
Clearly, if my hon. friend and I are speaking of the same document, and I think we are, the document was widely circulated. As I have said, it was sent to the regional directors and chiefs of Indian band councils, and was made available to all Indians through their band councils. There is nothing privileged about the document; it is not classified. Since the hon. member for Skeena has been so helpful in identifying the document, perhaps I might be allowed to table it in the House.
Before sitting down may I thank my hon. friend for helping to describe the document. He has been most helpful. Although his criticism may have been fair, and I concede that Members of Parliament have a responsibility in these matters, his criticism of departmental officials might have been more valid if he had taken a bit more care in drafting the notice of motion. Then, the particular document or memorandum he wanted might have been identified from among the hundreds of memoranda on the subject that are sent, and continue to be sent, to regional directors. These documents are meant to be a basis for consultation with Indians in their particular areas.

It is on the basis of this memorandum that discussions were to be held with the Indian people in connection with certain proposed modifications to the Indian Band Council grants program.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was pleased to hear the remarks made by the minister in introducing second reading of this bill. I am also gratified at the number of people who have received support under this act. The amendments to the act throw no light on what the act has done for children of war dead, but I think it is safe to say that under this legislation, as under other veterans legislation concerned with the education of veterans and the children of veterans, we have more for our money than is the case with most pieces of legislation passed by Parliament.
I think it is also true to say that no educational assistance provided under veterans affairs legislation has been more productive than the act we are now discussing. For example, take the case of a woman whose husband returned from overseas badly wounded and later died, leaving several small children. I suspect that those children's chances of going on to higher education on the amount of money the widow would receive under other pension legislation would be non-existent were it not for this particular act. As I say, the dollar value received for the money spent under this legislation has been exceedingly good.
I am pleased that in these amendments the minister has taken into consideration two matters that have radically changed in approach over the years. One concerns age requirement. An opportunity is being afforded children to attend school for longer than has been the case in the past. This provision is in keeping with modern times and is a change well worth making. The other matter relates to the person who is weak in a particular subject and it has cost him his year. There is a growing body of opinion that it is one's over-all educational qualifications that are important, and so long as one has a reasonable awareness of all subjects a student should be allowed to proceed to a higher education level and carry his one weak subject. Prior to these amendments such a person would not have qualified for assistance.
I suggest the minister could also have considered assisting education in institutions other than universities. I include courses of instruction at technical colleges. Many of our high schools are now offering courses in technical subjects, and a great deal of emphasis is put on taking full advantage of the natural ability of students in the field for which they are best equipped. Many of these students have yet to complete even their elementary
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Bechard) .1

education. In many cases where education is sought in the technical field beyond high school level assistance is not now available. I think the minister could have considered providing some assistance in these cases as well.
It is true that when this act was originally passed in 1953 the need was for assistance at the university level. Technical education in most provinces had not advanced to the level where it offered a major opportunity to most students. But today attendance at technical school beyond the elementary level of education costs just as much as for attending university, with the probable exception of the tuition fee. I suggest the minister could have put forward an amendment to assist a large segment of the population to take advantage of technical education in every province in Canada.
Neither of the amendments proposed by the minister offer assistance of this kind. I am sure most members feel that since this legislation is offering assistance to children of war dead, it is obviously coming to the end of its life. Today the child of a father killed overseas during the last war would be about 27 years old and with respect to him the provisions of the act are self-liquidating. However, since numbers of children will now qualify under the act because they are in receipt of a compassionate pension under the Pension Act, the need for this legislation will remain for some time.

This would allow students to attain higher educational standards in certain fields, including university degree courses following a number of years in an academic field. Mr. Speaker, I hesitated because I thought other hon. members would want to make some remarks about this bill. I want to take the opportunity to draw the minister's attention in a public way to something about which I have had correspondence with him. The minister has on four occasions said that the act has been changed
November 6, 1969	COMMONS
to expand facilities and to extend the assistance offered to groups which were heretofore excluded. There is still a deficiency within the act and its regulations; there is a disparity which is not corrected by the amendments now before us. The disparity occurs in respect of children now coming under the Pension Commission and children who receive benefits under Children of War Dead (Education Assistance) Act.
I have in mind those children who come within the ambit of the provisions of this act and attend institutions of higher learning than secondary schools. They do not receive assistance if the educational institution they attend does not have a requirement for a secondary school graduation certificate. In other words, if a student intends going to a university or college which requires a secondary school graduation certificate, he can receive assistance under the act. If a student wishes to attend an educational institution- say of a technical or vocational nature-other than a university, which might not have an entrance requirement including a certificate of graduation from a secondary school, assistance is not available.
I have exchanged correspondence with the minister in this regard. Let me put on the record part of what the minister said to me in a letter dated September 25 following representations made to him. In one paragraph of the letter he said:
-facilities for technological training and the broadening of the occupational fields in which such training is given can quite properly, I think, be described as remarkable in the past decade.

The majority of these newly developed courses require secondary school graduation as an entry condition, and it would be a retrogressive step to establish a lower criterion for the Children of War Dead (Education Assistance) Act at this time.
