speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION OF ADDITIONAL JUDGES IN ALBERTA AND ONTARIO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate you for taking the Chair again in this session of Parliament. Through you may I send my commendations to Mr. Speaker and the Deputy Speaker together with my best wishes as they preside over the chamber during this session.
Bill C-2 is adequately described in the explanatory note. However, I will say very briefly that authority is sought from Parliament for the provision of salaries for eight additional judges; two judges of the Supreme Court of Alberta, five judges of the county and district courts of Ontario and one judge of the district court of Alberta. I should like to mention for the information of the House that the number of judicial offices for the district court of Alberta was increased by way of provincial order in council. The order in council was passed by the government of Alberta, providing for an additional district judge of the southern part of Alberta, on February 11, 1969. The provision for increasing the number of judicial offices of the trial division of the Supreme Court of Alberta was made in a statute of that province which received royal assent on April 21 of this year. As I said, provision is also made in this bill for increasing by five the number of judicial offices in the county and district courts of Ontario, four for the county of York and one for the county of Carleton. The Ontario legislature provided for these additional judicial offices by a statute of the legislature which received royal assent on March 26 of this year.
From discussions I have had with my provincial counterparts, the attorneys general of Alberta and Ontario, concerning the administration of justice in those provinces and based on the information that I receive from time to
614

November 6, 1969
Judges Act
time from the legal profession and from the public generally, I am satisfied that these increases are warranted. They are necessary to deal effectively with the additional volume of judicial business and litigation in those provinces that must be transacted in the public interest. I am satisfied, therefore, that Parliament would be justified in authorizing an increase in the provisions for the salaries of these judges.
In recent times I have received submissions from the Canadian Bar Association and from other quarters indicating that in the opinion of the bar it is time we began to think about further changes in the Judges Act. This bill is a simple one again this year. It provides for an increased number of judges, but the time will come very soon-I think by the next session of Parliament-when we should think seriously about fundamental amendments to the Judges Act.
The question of salaries is one which we shall have to consider. I felt that it was not appropriate this year to come before Parliament and ask for any increase in the salaries of judges in the country. But I say frankly to Parliament that it is becoming increasingly difficult for me to persuade some of the leading candidates for judicial office, particularly lawyers who have had experience before the courts, younger men between 40 and 50 years of age who could make a great contribution to the bench and thereby to the administration of justice, to accept judicial office.

speechtext: Or parliamentary office for that matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION OF ADDITIONAL JUDGES IN ALBERTA AND ONTARIO
speechtext:
I will take that as read. Those men between 40 and 50 have children who are usually at the high school or university stage, and are therefore at their maximum financial exposure in those years. When one considers that the current provisions for widows and dependent children are ludicrously low, it is often very difficult to persuade them to accept the office. The widow's pension is two-ninths of two-thirds of the judge's salary, and many women are now living close to penury. However, as I said, I felt that this year was not the proper time to broach the subject. But I say to the House that we will be looking very seriously into the matter of salaries, pensions and expenses during the coming year because I think it is important that we attract the best men and women we can to serve on the bench in Canada. In order to do that one has to offer remuneration that is at least somewhat competitive with what they might otherwise 
receive. There are a few matters that I would like to mention briefly for the purpose of informing the House about a number of initiatives that we have taken during the last year with respect to the judiciary.

First, I should mention that we have set up language courses for judges. I must inform the House that, between July 20 and August 8, a series of classes was given successfully in the capital city of Quebec for 24 judges of the provincial Superior Courts.
I am glad to mention, Mr. Speaker, that judges from seven out of ten provinces attended these classes. The courses were given by the federal school of languages. These are preliminary courses of necessity and these judges as well as those from the federal courts will be able to attend French classes in their own district and if they take an immersion course in a school of languages, I think that they will be able to improve their ability to speak or at least to understand the other language.
Bilingual facilities will also be available to French-speaking judges of the Superior Courts and we are confident that our program for French-speaking and English-speaking judges will be made available to all members of the judiciary.
In the near future we hope to be in a position to make these courses available to all district and county judges. Obviously, these courses have to be organized so as not to affect the proper administration of justice. Therefore, a schedule of classes has to be arranged with the co-operation of the chief justices of the country.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)

I also wish to say something about the Canadian Judicial Conference which was held for the first time this past summer in the city of Toronto. We sent the judges back to school. I might say that this was done with the full, enthusiastic co-operation of the Chief Justices of the country. The course was sponsored by the federal government. It was established by the Conference of Chief Justices of Canada. The council of the conference is composed of Chief Justice Gale of Ontario as chairman, with Associate Chief Justice Challies of Quebec as vice-chairman. The balance of the council is composed of Chief Justice Smith of Alberta, Chief Justice Culliton of Saskatchewan and Chief Justice Cowan of Nova Scotia. This council convened the first seminar which
November 6, 19G9



began on August 14 in the city of Toronto. It lasted for an entire week and 24 judges from all parts of Canada attended.
1 was particularly glad that Mr. Justice William Morrow, territorial judge of the Northwest Territories, was among these 24 judges. I would hope that because of the remoteness of his particular circuit he would be able to attend these courses at least every second year in order that he could be brought into contact with his brother judges across the country who have more opportunity to converse with each and keep abreast of the law. In fact, he made such an impression upon his brother judges that they have asked him to join the faculty of the seminar next year. I would suggest that Mr. Justice Henry Madison of the Yukon be invited to attend these seminars on alternate years. I understand that the seminar will be an annual event sponsored by the Council of Chief Justices.
I would like to read into the record the faculty for the seminar this year which consisted of the following persons: Chief Justice Tremblay of Montreal, Chief Justice Challies of Montreal, Chief Justice Cowan of Halifax, Mr. Justice Laskin of Toronto, Mr. Justice Hartt of Toronto, Mr. Justice McFarlane of Vancouver, Mr. Justice Brooke of Toronto, Dean G. E. LeDain, Q.C., of Toronto, Professor John Edwards of Toronto, Professor D. Mendes da Costa of Toronto, and the Dean was H. Allan Leal, Q.C., of Toronto.
I wish to thank publicly the members of the faculty for participating in what I think is a very useful initiative in Canadian judicial practice. It is my information, not only from the council but from the judges who attended the seminar, that they all benefited individually from the course. One of their particularly lively discussions concerned public relations, and I understand they had a stimulating discussion with Mr. Jack Dennett and Mr. Ray Corelli, two well known representatives of the newspaper world in the city of Toronto.
Among the subjects discussed at the seminar were criminal law and procedure, divorce, evidence, administrative bodies, the preparation and writing of judgments, judicial behaviour and recent trends in the law of contract and tort. I would hope we could reach a stage where once every five years every high court judge in the country would be able to go back to school to continue his legal training, not just for a period of one week but for, say, three weeks, and that subjects that are of social concern and subjects 21362-401
Judges Act
of current human confrontation before the courts would be researched.
I believe that the Canadian Judicial Conference inaugurated last year fills a very definite void that has existed in this country for a great many years in the area of judicial training. We are trying to improve our law schools and make their curricula more relevant. We are trying to inaugurate courses in consumer law, courses on law as it affects the poor, on law to protect the debtor as well as the creditor, the borrower as well as the lender. I believe that the legal profession in certain parts of the country is becoming alive to its responsibilities as a profession and is recognizing that society as a whole is the client of the law. I am delighted to see that the judges of this country are becoming more responsive to the new urges for change under the law. The Canadian Judicial Conference will serve as a refresher course for those who have sat on the bench for some time.

speechtext:
We started this in a limited way, but as I have said I hope we will expand it so that every judge in the country gets this refresher course once every five years. I think this is important because I think the judges, and the bench as a whole, must realize that in an era where there is a crisis of legitimacy, of authority, there is no institution in this country that is immune from criticism, and the bench must also respond to these urges for change and social responsibility. The seminar will be held in the city of Montreal next year and a completely different group of judges will attend on that occasion.
I should also mention that the annual conference of the Chief Justices of Canada met in Edmonton this year on September 28, 29 and 30. This conference is now well established and a decision was taken at this year's meeting to convene next year's meeting in Newfoundland. This conference enables all the Chief Justices to meet to discuss problems that are common to them in relation to the administration of justice. They find that they

November 6, 1969
Judges Act
are able to assist one another greatly by their free exchange of ideas. They are able to carry back to their own respective benches various suggestions relating to procedures and administration, and interpretations of the law, that have considerable value to all members of the bench.
I should like at this time to make a brief reference to the question of judicial appointments. As you will recall, Mr. Speaker, I went into this matter rather fully last year. We have continued the practice of consulting, prior to recommending appointments to the bench, the Judicial Committee of the Canadian Bar Association. Aside from that, I consult the members of the provincial bars concerned and sometimes members of the bench who have the opportunity of judging who are the competent counsel appearing before them. We consult as widely as we can in the community. But I want to add that of course the final responsibility for making a recommendation to the Governor in Council remains mine. I do not intend to shirk that responsibility or delegate it to any other body. I believe that I should take the heat in the legislature for the appointments whether they are good or bad. I might say that no candidate for the bench whom the committee of the Canadian Bar Association judged not qualified received an appointment to the bench since my appointment to this portfolio. In other words only those whom the bar committee judged to be qualified received nomination and appointment.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, I am sure hon. members will recall that for the first time in the history of this country a lady was appointed to one of the high courts in Canada, the Superior Court of the Province of Quebec. Madame Rejeanne Colas is an outstanding woman. She graduated top of her class at the law school of the University of Montreal in 1952 and practised law for 16 or 17 years before appointment to the bench. She has three children, was president of Les Clubs Feminins de la Province de Quebec, and chairman of the Canadian Bar Association Committee on Family Law. She has made an outstanding contribution to the bench in the six months since her appointment, particularly with reference to interpretation of the new Divorce Act.
Mr. Speaker, I should now like to mention the Supreme Court and Exchequer Court in relation to the Official Languages Act. Members of the House will recall that sections 5 and 11 of this act impose obligations upon the

federal judiciary. I have taken appropriate steps to see that arrangements are made to meet the requirements in section 5 to permit simultaneous translation in the Supreme Court and Exchequer Court. Both languages have enjoyed equal rights before the federal courts of this country but the additional requirements in sections 5 and 11 make some adjustments necessary. I am informed that these are well in hand. I have also been considering the usefulness of certain regulations on judicial proceedings which might be made by order in council under section 11 (5) of the Official Languages Act in order to facilitate the application of section 11 (2) respecting simultaneous translation. These rules, if made, would apply to all courts of record established pursuant to an act of the Parliament of Canada as well as to the Supreme Court and Exchequer Court.
There are also courts in the Yukon and Northwest Territories to be considered. I have caused enquiries to be made as to what arrangements will be necessary for them in order to meet the exigencies of the Official Languages Act. Here, too, the matter seems to be well in hand. We have arranged to appoint Mr. Justice Dechene of the Alberta Supreme Court a deputy judge for the Northwest Territories, and we are attempting to provide court staff so that it will be possible to have proceedings in the French language where necessary without obligatory recourse to simultaneous translation in the French language. It is not yet settled whether similar arrangements will have to be made in the Yukon Territory. However, translation of the judgements of both these courts will be made available as well as facilities for simultaneous translation where required.
Mr. Speaker, that is a small report to the shareholders in the country through their representatives in this House in so far as the judiciary under the authority of the federal government is concerned. But the administration of justice is wider than that, and sometimes I find it restricting and even frustrating that the daffy operation of the courts falls within provincial jurisdiction in both criminal and civil matters. Whereas all criminal law in statute form rests with Parliament, prosecution under the Criminal Code is the responsibility of the provincial attorneys general. But there are problems within the administration of justice that, while provincial in content, are so national in scope that sometimes I find it necessary to communicate with the several attorneys general. Indeed, when they were here at the beginning of the week discussing
November 6, 1969

the Charter of Human Rights we considered the possibility of convening a meeting of all attorneys general federal and provincial to deal with national problems relating to the administration of justice.
I am concerned about the delays in our courts, whether the responsibility lies with the judiciary, or the bar, lawyers who amongst themselves conveniently arrange to postpone cases. In the Department of Justice in Ottawa we are exploring the uses of the computer in the land. I think it could be used a great deal in promoting the administration of justice at the provincial level. In order to set to rest the fears of the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) let me say that we do not intend to replace lawyers, we just intend to explore some improvements. I am convinced that if justice in the city of Toronto or Montreal were put to a computer for the purpose of ascertaining who is responsible for the delay in our courts, the answer might be the same as that found in Philadelphia where delays were traced to just one or two law firms who were digesting too much business. But I do think we should pinpoint the responsibility for the delays.
We must consider the effectiveness of right to counsel. We must also consider the very serious problem which is building up with respect to the Divorce Act. Dissolving a marriage does not solve the problems of maintenance, alimony and custody of children. These matters often have to be decided by separate courts in the same jurisdiction and it is not unusual to have the same matrimonial situation simultaneously before two or three courts. All the legal consequences of divorce and marriage should somehow be co-ordinated better than they are at present.
Mr. Speaker, these are some of the matters relating to the administration of justice and the appointment of judges which fall within the general scope of this bill. In any event, my brother attorneys general are agreeable to a conference and I hope we can hold it late in the spring. I thank the House very much for its attention.

I have the keen attention of my friends to the left who are already evincing an interest in what I am going to say before I even say it. The distinguished and
Judges Act
learned critic for this party is at present engaged in examining other legislation which the minister will be presenting to the House leader, and this has catapulted me into making a speech. I was glad to hear the minister engage in a rather extracurricular discussion-no one is objecting to it-but the question of the appointment of judges should not be any bar to the minister, to members of the opposition or backbenchers on the government side dealing with this matter in some detail.
Mr. Speaker, anyone who has seen on television or read in the press in the past year of the riots and violence which have taken place throughout the western world will have wondered whether the courts are going to have a place in society as we know it. Is there a place for those delegated by society to the decision-making process in the judiciary to determine the rights of the parties, having in mind the stresses of modern times? Is there a real place for a man learned in the law to calmly and dispassionately make a decision in disputes arising between citizens or between citizens and the state? To some of us this would not appear necessary. People have taken to the streets. The demonstration which has sometimes become violent has counter-balanced the machinery our society has established for dealing with such problems. I was glad to hear the minister give some indication of his thinking in this regard. It was not the government's thinking, but his own. His remarks gave us an insight and will enable us to judge what we may look forward to in this regard in the next year or two.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
We must appoint to the judiciary people who are not only learned in the law but are knowledgeable about society and the frailties of human nature. The men we appoint must be those who can sit on a dais and weigh, evaluate and assess the conflicts between human beings and the differences between them. They will listen to people who challenge the rights of governments and the rights of big corporations. I think no society will remain free and good unless we evolve methods of selecting people of this kind for judicial appointment.
May I digress and say that I have sometimes heard in different parts of Canada and in this House the suggestion that those who serve in the public life of this country, our politicians in other words, should not be made judges. I disagree with that. I am not saying that one's participation in public life by itself

November 6, 1969
Judges Act
is a mark of distinction and should automatically mean that one may be elevated to the bench. Men in public life have often been elevated. I submit that men in public life gain an insight into human nature, and a politician has that faculty. The man who has sat on the opposition benches and had to contend with the monolithic apparatus of government makes a very good judge-and please do not think I am preaching for a call, Mr. Speaker. It is bad enough for one to have to sit here and to listen to some of the speeches. At least we can walk out occasionally, but unfortunately judges cannot do that and are compelled to stay and listen to what is being said.
I make this comment only because I have heard it repeated frequently in this House during the last 10 or 15 years that the man in public life, even though he may have all the other necessary qualifications, should not be elevated to the bench. I disagree with that. In making judicial appointments we recognize that the government of the day will, all things being equal, probably appoint its supporters to the bench. I do not quarrel with that, provided the appointees have all other necessary qualifications. I have discussed this matter with the minister from time to time and will continue to do so as objectively as I can.
If society as we know it is to endure, we must have a free Parliament and a free, independent, very learned and knowledgeable judiciary. Any minister of justice attempting to acquire for the bench of this country people of that character will have my support. While it is very nice to have bilingual judges, if the government must choose between two men, let it choose the good judge. If the judges appointed are bilingual, so much the better. But if you have a man who speaks French and no English and he would make a good judge, I say that you should by all means appoint him. Similarly, if you have a lawyer who speaks English but not too much French and he would make a good judge, by all means appoint him. If you can find a man who speaks both languages, that is fine.
In my experience of the past 40 years I have never come across a case-and I was substantially involved in counsel work- where a person charged with an offence or involved in civil proceedings was unable to secure from the court, upon request, the fullest opportunity to have made available to him in the language of his choice all statements nnd evidence given before the court. In all

instances persons are made fully aware of what is taking place. As this country progresses we may reach the stage where all those appointed to the judiciary will be bilingual, although I think it may be many years before that happens. I urge the minister to exercise the utmost caution in his appointments and not let his desire to appoint a bilingual judge interfere with his need to appoint a good judge.
How judges behave is very important. I recall that as a young law student I appeared in a case-I was not appearing on my own but had a watching brief-involving a woman who was charged with being the keeper of a bawdy house. Something turned upon whether the particular house had stairs at the back, and a lengthy examination was conducted on this point. Finally the judge turned to counsel and said, "Surely you can tell the court whether the stairs are in fact there." The accused woman turned and said to the judge, "But Your Lordship was there last night. You should know that."
Next I wish to speak about our divorce courts. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was Minister of Justice many of us in the House said that jurisdiction to try divorces should not be restricted to Supreme Court judges and that the backlog of human misery which had been built up over the course of years would create many judicial problems. Some provinces take the position that certain leading cases give their county judges jurisdiction to try divorces. I think it would have been better if Parliament had made a unilateral declaration that county and Supreme Court judges can try divorce cases. May I repeat what I have said before. I see no reason for the present distinction between judges. I think we pay Supreme Court judges $26,000 a year, and county and district court judges $19,000 a year. Can you measure the value of justice by the amount you pay a member of the bar?
For a great many years, both as a member of the bar and as a bencher of the Law Society of Alberta, as well as a Member of Parliament, I said that this distinction should be abolished. If the Government of Canada acting on instructions from the Parliament of Canada has the right to appoint judges to courts of record, why should it say, "You, John Brown, with your knowledge and capacity are limited to trying civil cases not involving more than so many thousands of dollars and criminal cases of certain types. But you, Bill Smith, have complete jurisdiction over everything." Justice should not be
November 6, 1969

valued in those terms. I urge the minister to consider abolishing the distinction between county and Supreme Court judges. If a member of the bar has in the opinion of the minister the qualifications necessary to adjudicate in a civil capacity between people and people, people and corporations, people and the government and in criminal cases, he should have the capacity to try divorce cases whether or not he is a county court or Supreme Court judge. Our only reason for maintaining the distinction is that it existed at the time of confederation and we have continued it to the present time. I suggest there should be only one category of judge rather than a division between county court, district court and Supreme Court.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
The minister mentioned judges attending school. I think this is a very good idea. All people in authority should go to school. From time to time even the cabinet should take a little time off and go to school to learn something. They might even learn to answer questions, Mr. Speaker.

There are good reasons for this. While we should strive to develop jurisprudence which works toward achieving certain common objectives, nevertheless because human beings are what they are it is not easy to say, for example, that a person who has committed a criminal offence in the province of Ontario should receive the same punishment as a person who committed the same offence in the province of Alberta. Circumstances and environment differ. Each case must be considered entirely on its own merits.
I am nauseated when I hear people talking about uniformity of sentence. There can be no such thing as uniformity of sentence. Sentencing is one of the most important parts of our criminal jurisdiction. Having found a person guilty of a criminal offence, a most searching inquiry consistent with equity must be made into the background of the relevant, surrounding circumstances. I consider it quite improper for the Prime Minister or any minister to suggest that with respect to offences committed under the Narcotic Control Act or any section of the Criminal Code there must be uniformity of sentence. I believe the minister, in response to questions the other day, made this quite plain. There can be no more uniformity of sentence than there can be uniformity of individuals.
Judges Act
I think it would probably serve a good purpose if judges did get together to discuss among themselves their experiences and problems and listen to lectures. Nevertheless, there are limits to this type of practice. It is about time this House became a more effective and active instrument in the formulation of policy with regard to judges. I think it might be advisable if judges appeared before a committee of this House in Ottawa or somewhere else and discussed with the members of the committee, in an informal way, some of the problems which they as the judiciary have encountered. I think this practice would be very useful.
This may appear irrelevant, although it is in the context of what I have been saying, but I feel a committee should be charged with the continuing responsibility of examining our criminal law and all other types of law reform. The committee should be maintained through the course of Parliament, not only to deal with various bills which the minister presents but to deal with other matters of this kind. I think it would be most useful if in fact judges appeared before such a committee from time to time. The hearings could even be held in camera. In this way the committee would have the benefit of the judges' views.
I wish to stress the great importance of the character and type of people who are appointed to the bench. This matter has already been mentioned by the minister. We may talk about anti-bugging devices, matters of defence and secrecy and the problems of the unfortunate people who have become drug addicts, but in the final analysis the extent to which any society continues to survive depends upon those people who have been elevated to judge their fellow human beings. Nothing can be more important than to ensure that the quality and character of these people remains at the very highest level.

I do not read the act in that way. I followed it closely and even urged an amendment in this House so that it would be clear there would be concurrent jurisdiction in county court judges. The predecessor of the minister, now the Prime Minister, said that although all the advice is to the contrary, we were not prepared to do this. I suggested the requisite amendment should be to the Divorce Act. It should be clear to the province that there is a designation of jurisdiction. There have been delays and attendant expense in the way these matters have been dealt with in the past.
It makes sense when county court judges have this added jurisdiction they will carry a heavier burden than is the case at the present time. I make no apology for approving the addition of these needed judicial officers even

at a time when in the interest of controlling inflation the economy axe is being used. It would be false economy to overburden the judicial process by not being ready to make additional judicial appointments when they are required.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
There are other fields where the same principle applies. Parole is under the jurisdiction of his colleague, the Solicitor General (Mr. Mcllraith), though I know the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) has particular interest in that subject. However, I suggest it is false economy not to increase substantially the number of parole officers. Every parole officer on the job saves the country a considerable amount of money, because they are able to service those who otherwise would be in detention. Certainly they can look after people on parole better than if they were still in detention. I hope that no attempt will be made to wield the economy axe as far as the appointment of additional staff in parole institutions is concerned.
The appointment of judges has been discussed, and in this regard I want to say something that I think the minister will be pleased to hear. As far as I know, since the minister has been Minister of Justice appointments to the bench have been of a very high calibre. The appointments have not been political appointments. May I congratulate him on those appointments of which I am aware, though I am not aware of all of them. However, I suggest it is simply not good enough for the minister to perform in the manner he is. If another minister were in his place we might again run into the sort of pork-barrel system that prevailed for many generations when people were appointed to the bench on the basis of political patronage. There has been no greater scandal in the judicial history of our country than this tendency that has existed in the past.
I am happy to say that I do not believe this practice exists today. Indeed, I hope it will never be resuscitated in the future. However, it is the system itself that requires change. We should not have to depend on the good intentions of ministers of justice who are from time to time appointed. The present minister says that he consults the bar associations and other qualified people with regard to judicial appointment, but I suggest some system be worked out under which the temptation to use these appointments for political purposes is removed.
November 6, 1969

I am aware of the conscious effort of the minister to take politics out of these appointments, but I hope he will not think this will be achieved merely by adopting his present practice for just a little while. I have seen new ministers of justice come to their portfolio with the highest intentions. The first few appointments made are admirable, but then as they linger on and the demands of former supporters become more insistent, later appointments do not reach the same high calibre of the earlier ones. I hope this will not happen as far as this minister is concerned, but I warn him that it has happened before and it might happen again. I suggest that while the opportunity presents itself he should ensure that some system of consultation is firmly embedded in the legislation.
I was delighted to hear that judges were going to be sent to school again. It has been my experience at the bar, especially when I was a young lawyer, that very few judges would have the humility to return to school. They seemed to know almost everything and did not require any instruction from counsel; at least, that could be said of some of them. I was glad to hear the minister say that some of their instruction would be in social subjects. I believe that past legal training has completely failed to instil any adequate social awareness in those who are called to the bar. They do not have any adequate knowledge of the modern social sciences to assist them to do their job. I hope that when judges return to school they will take these courses seriously; that they will be attended not by just a few conscientious judges but that they will be regularly attended by all judges.

Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to learn that some English-speaking judges have taken French immersion courses.

I see no purpose in detaining the House longer by discussing this bill. As I said at the beginning, the subject is not earth-shaking. I think we might properly pass the bill, and may I thank the minister for taking the time and trouble to tell us something about how his department is approaching the whole question of judicial appointments and activities. I must say I was encouraged by what he said.

Mr. Speaker, while I do not wish to put myself forward as a connoisseur of the French language, I had to avail myself of the services of

the translator to appreciate the effort of the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) at the close of his remarks.
I should also say that since the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) had occasion during the course of his speech to mention the present justices of the territorial courts in the Northwest Territories and Yukon territory, I would be very remiss if I did not take this occasion, one that I think is very appropriate, to commemorate the passing this past year of the first judge of the territorial court of the Northwest Territories, the Hon. Jack Sissons. I had the pleasure and privilege of articling in law at Lethbridge at a time when Judge Sissons was chief judge of the district court, and a very good friend of mine he was. He was also a very good friend of the native people of the Northwest Territories. I understand his popularity here was somewhat more circumscribed. I do not propose to attempt to discuss the judicial situation in the province of Ontario, but I should like to elaborate to some extent on a subject opened up by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) during his speech. I refer to the rationale for the division of the two courts in the province of Alberta.
By chapter 4 of the Statutes of Alberta, 1907, the district court was established on the basis that in every judicial district there would be a resident-I underline the word "resident"-district court judge who could exercise his jurisdiction, in the absence of a special direction, only within the judicial district in which he held his appointment. His civil jurisdiction in trial matters went to a maximum of $400.
At that time the Supreme Court, consisting of five judges, exercised both trial and appeal jurisdiction. There were nine judicial districts and two sub-judicial districts. Of these, the more populous were Calgary, with a population of 31,800; Edmonton, with a population of 20,500, including Strathcona; Lethbridge, with 6,200; and Medicine Hat with 4,300. The other judicial districts were Athabasca, Wetaskiwin, Red Deer, Stettler and Macleod.
A resident judge in a community of small population could become involved in the community life and intimately known by his neighbours. Therefore, it was not difficult to understand that it was in the interests of justice that an independent, removed judicial personage should come to the community to deal with the more serious civil and criminal matters and matters involving jury trials. With the difficulties of transportation it is

November 6, 1969
Judges Act
easy to understand why district court judges were also required to be resident judges. However, in 1933, by chapter 15 of the Statutes of Alberta the province was divided into district courts for northern and southern Alberta. The judges appointed had jurisdiction throughout the district; that is to say, judges appointed as district court judges for southern Alberta had complete jurisdiction throughout southern Alberta, and this was the case with the district court judges in northern Alberta district courts.
In effect, this meant the disappearance of resident judges as such. At the present time Alberta is served by eight district court judges for the district of northern Alberta, all of whom reside in Edmonton; and by six district court judges for the district of southern Alberta, four of whom reside in Calgary and two in Lethbridge. The district court judges in northern Alberta serve six judicial districts, and by order in council are required to hold court in 12 centres. The district court judges in southern Alberta serve six judicial districts as well, and by order in council are required to hold court in 19 centres. In each case, the centres other than those where the judges reside are served by judges travelling to these centres at the times scheduled to hear chamber applications, hold civil and criminal trials, deal with matters of adoption and wardship, probate, administration and the passing of accounts. In the matter of chamber applications, and in civil trials, the judges are frequently required to act and exercise jurisdiction as local judges of the Supreme Court.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
The jurisdictional wall between the two courts, the district and Supreme Court, is an odd thing. The numerous overlappings and contradictions make it appear that it is something without any real, present day reason. The District Courts Act limits the trial jurisdiction to cases involving a monetary value of $2,000, but the Seizures Act gives complete jurisdiction to the district court. This jurisdiction involves the determination, in a summary way, with affadavit or viva voce evidence, of such matters as the right to make seizure, the amount payable between the parties or the ownership of goods. There have been in Calgary cases under this act where the question for determination was the ownership of $1 million worth of machinery and the ownership of $750,000 worth of bowling equipment. These cases were heard and 
determined in a summary way by the district court. The Surrogate Courts Act gives to judges of the district court jurisdiction in "all matters arising out of or connected with the issue and revocation of grants of probate and administration" and confers the rights and powers of the Supreme Court and of the judges and officers thereof.
There has never been any limitation of the value of a probate or administration with which a district court judge could deal, although in the past, before the Surrogate Courts Act, certain matters had to be referred to the Supreme Court. Under the Domestic Relations Act, Supreme Court judges hearing divorce actions have dealt with the question of the custody of the children and have awarded custody to one or other parent. No order for such custody is ever final and may be referred back to the court in the event of any change in the circumstances of the respective parties. But under the Child Welfare Act a judge of the district court has the power, and it must be frequently exercised, to make a child a permanent ward of the Crown and permit his or her adoption by other persons. In the exercise of this power a district court judge may make an order for permanent wardship which by section 32 of the Child Welfare Act takes precedence over any order for custody given by anyone else. With the consent of the parties a district court judge may as local judge of the Supreme Court hear and determine any action brought in the Supreme Court, and in such case he has the same powers as a judge of the Supreme Court. The district court has concurrent jurisdiction with the Supreme Court in all matters except capital offences and trial by jury.
In southern Alberta, district court judges serve six judicial districts and hold court in 19 centres. Two of these are not visited with any regularity because they are close to other centres and the solicitors bring their work to these other centres. But the other 17 are served regularly. The judicial centres, six of them, are served regularly by the trial division of the Supreme Court. In Lethbridge, for example, where there are two resident district court judges and where the public is well served by them, the Supreme Court will attend four times in the spring term to do those things which a district court judge could do if he had the jurisdiction. Medicine Hat is served weekly by one or other of the district court judges from Lethbridge. Three times during the spring term judges of the
November 6, 1969

Supreme Court are required to go to Medicine Hat to do those things which the limit of jurisdiction prevents the district court judge from doing when he is there at the same time.
The district court judges from Calgary serve Hanna and Drumheller, both of which are judicial centres of separate judicial districts, once a month. In the spring term judges of the Supreme Court must go twice to Drumheller, in each case within a few days of the district court judge, to do those things which the division of the courts makes necessary. The same situation holds true in the judicial districts of northern Alberta outside the city of Edmonton.
It is significant that much of the work done by the judges of the district court in these outlying points is done in the exercise of their jurisdiction as local judges of the Supreme Court. But those functions which can be performed only by judges of the Supreme Court are not performed at those centres to which district court judges go, which are not the centres of judicial districts. Banff, Brooks, Cardston, Blairmore, Claresholm, to name just a few, although they are served regularly by the district court must bring all Supreme Court matters to Calgary, to Medicine Hat, to Lethbridge or to Fort Macleod. An amalgamation of the two courts would not diminish the service; it would only do away with the duplication, which is costly and senseless.
The qualifications for appointment as judge of the district court are the same as those for appointment as judge of the Supreme Court. The law and its application is the same in both courts, the rules of evidence are the same, the rules of court apply to both courts and the rules of procedure are the same. But the separation of the courts and the limits of jurisdiction placed on the district court leave the public with the impression that there is a lesser brand of justice in a lower court.
I realize that this a matter for reform by provincial government and I hope that with the endorsement of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) the Attorney General of Alberta will get the idea that this might be a good thing to do. I certainly hope the Minister of Justice is prepared to go along with any such action. The only cost to us is related to extra salaries. There are not too many things which western Canada feels it can learn from the province of Quebec, but we can look upon the actions of Quebec in this, regard as a very progressive step.

Mr. Speaker, if w.e had not been enticed to participate in this debate perhaps we would have dealt with the matter by now. A couple of points mentioned by the minister deserve elaboration. I do not suggest he did not cover the subject completely, but there is room for another expansion or point of view regarding the change that will take place. This is true particularly in view of the minister's suggestion that at the next session or some time in the near future there will be an overhaul of the Judges Act in terms of philosophy and structure rather than just changes in respect of bits and pieces of the act.
At the outset I would say in respect of the matter of judges salaries that so far as I am concerned, it is extremely important. Their job is in many cases extremely difficult. If there is only the matter of salaries involved, and by increasing salaries we can obtain a high standard and quality of judges in our courts, by all means raise the salaries. We should not be hesitant in this regard.
I know the government is sensitive about curtailing inflation through a reduction of government expenditure. The minister should not be timid in this area, because it is a very important field. Judges are public servants who deal with interpretation regarding the rights, functions and the position of society. The minister mentioned that some judges have recently gone to school.

speechtext: I said they have gone back to school.

subtopic: PROVISION OF ADDITIONAL JUDGES IN ALBERTA AND ONTARIO
speechtext:
I prefer my original phrase-some judges have recently gone to school, particularly in terms of bilingualism. In this regard many judges are lacking education in terms of the humanities of our society. Many of them are too damn legalistic and narrow minded when it comes to interpreting the law. They have no concept whatever of individual feelings. Many of them operate simply on the basis of the criminal law and mete out the full extent of the penalty the law provides. It is in this area that I think an element of education is necessary.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
Since I am not one of those who has any desire to be a judge, nor the opportunity since I am not in a field or activity that would lead to it, perhaps my remarks about judges may not be as precise as those of a lawyer. Quite frankly, however, I think there are too few judges in our court system and in our

November 6, 1969
Judges Act
society who have an all-embracing approach. There are too many judges, to put it the other way, who apply statutes universally whether they are dealing with the most violent criminal cases that come before them or with a young citizen who is appearing in court on a first offence for a minor, insignificant demeanor. There is a danger on the part of judges -and on the part of magistrates who do not fall within the jurisdiction here-to apply a sort of "two-bit" lecture approach without any concern for the individual or what is involved in a social or humanitarian sense.
I believe there is a tendency on the part of the courts and judges to disregard completely the whole social area of use or misuse of drugs. The misuse of drugs has reached fantastic proportions by any comparison with the past, and it has reached fantastic proportions in any comparison with age groups that use narcotics or hallucinatory drugs of all kinds now and those who used them in the past. In fact, government itself has today moved into this area, albeit on a scant basis, without too much understanding of what is involved in respect of the individual. How can one urge the judiciary to have any concern about this problem when they are faced with a particular law which they must enforce? I believe the judges, in the field of drug use and abuse, think in terms of the full impact of the criminal law against the offender and in the context that the penalty must be a preventive and deterrent measure. I believe it can be reasonably and logically argued that there is no connection whatever, in the field of drug use and misuse, between the deterrent concept and the actual use of the drug.
It is true that judges are enforcing the law as it is. Nonetheless, there is a certain psychology involved. The idea would seem to be that so long as the individual is behind bars and is in jail, he is not using drugs. Although that is not always the case, it is at least the case in theory. We have read of instances where judges, in meting out offences for a criminal act, will make the senseless statement that they are sentencing an individual to a particular institution because there he will have an opportunity to learn a trade. We have also read about judges meting out sentences to mentally or emotionally disturbed individuals who will make this sort of gracious remark, "I am sentencing you to this particular institution so that you will receive psychiatric help". Anyone who has paid the least attention to what goes on in our penal institutions is aware that the judges just do not know what they are talking about when

they make such declarations when sentencing people to penal institutions. They hope the person will receive psychiatric treatment or learn a trade so that they will become worthwhile members of society.
If judges were to go back to school, I think one of the requirements should be that they spend a certain period in our penal institutions which deal with young offenders. This should not be a casual visit which they would make when everything would be laid out and everything that was undesirable would be kept out of the way. Rather, it should be an extended visit in the form of an immersion course so that they would have an opportunity to find out what goes on in penal institutions. In this way a judge who hands down a sentence that an individual is to be incarcerated in jail would at least know through some association with the institution, from having visited there on a number of occasions, to what he is sentencing the individual. He might thereby have a more human attitude about the sentence he is meting out.
I do not think too many people will disagree with what I am about to say. Certainly some members of the House who are lawyers have spoken on this subject. We have two types of justice. Even though the standard of law may be the same, the justice which is meted out to the rich is different from the type of justice meted out to the poor. I am sure that from his activity in the legal field the minister is aware of cases where the person charged with an offence, because he did not have a fair amount of money at his disposal, was not able to arrange for the best hearing or obtain the best lawyer to fight his case through the legal system and the loopholes which exist in it.
There are in our society many people who do not have sufficient understanding of what is involved in court procedure. These people sometimes appear unrepresented in court either because of threats by the R.C.M.P. or perhaps because of promises of some sort of act of justice. They lack an understanding of their position, appear in court and plead guilty to charges of which they are in fact not guilty. Had they had the money with which to obtain proper legal assistance, in many instances they would never have been convicted.
So there is in the very practice of it, one type of justice for the rich and another for the poor. I believe this is something which must be looked at. I put forward these few ideas from the limited experience I have in
November 6, 1969

the courts and the legal system in the hope that they might have some effect on what is finally transformed into law when the philosophy relating to judges and the manner in which they enforce the law is considered.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State. In view of the fact that when the Manitoba legislature amended the provincial Elections Act to provide for voting at age 18 it also included a provision to make it possible for persons who are so disabled they cannot get to the polls to vote by mail, I wonder whether the federal government would consider making a similar recommendation so far as the federal Elections Act is concerned?
The Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) replied that he was not responsible for amendments to the Elections Act and that I should put my question to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald). However, that is a minor point and I am delighted to see the President of the Privy Council here tonight to respond to my question.
Mr. Speaker, it is a fact that the Manitoba legislature at a recent special session did pass Bill 38, entitled an act to amend the Elections Act. This bill makes two changes. On the one hand it lowers the voting age for provincial elections in Manitoba to 18 and, in addition, it includes a provision under which persons who are physically incapacitated may cast their vote by mail. The arrangements, of course, are spelled out in Manitoba's Bill 38 and are similar to arrangements made for members of the armed forces to vote in the federal election and the arrangements made in some other provinces for absentee voting.
However, the details are not important; what is important is that something has been done. In Manitoba persons who are physically incapacitated and therefore through no fault of their own are unable to go to the polls will be able to exercise their franchise in provincial elections in my province. It is my earnest hope that a similar provision will be included in the Canada Elections Act, and that this will be one of the results of the study to that legislation now being given by the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.

The problem of navigation on the Mackenzie River affects far fewer people than does the situation in the port of Vancouver, but for those people along the Mackenzie River and part of the Northwest Territories it is far more important. That is why I insisted upon the problem being ventilated. There is a problem in that area. I do not suppose many hon. members are aware of what has happened, but with a great fanfare the province of British Columbia constructed a huge hydro-electric dam on the Peace River at Partridge

It must be remembered that under the Navigable Waters Protection Act, protection must be provided. The act envisages protection of downstream interests when obstructions on navigable rivers are erected. This protection is not limited to those years when there is sufficient rainfall and adequate water resources. You have to take it by and large, good years and bad. It is said that this year there was a deficiency in rainfall. But what we saw, Mr. Speaker, was a deficiency in the water levels of the Athabasca River, as evidenced this spring. There was a deficiency in the level of the Mackenzie River, particularly this fall, for navigation purposes downstream, to such an extent that a crown company, Northern Transportation, had to make a public statement that it would have to undertake many hundreds of thousands of dollars of expenditure to clear the Sans Sault rapids for navigation purposes if it were to fulfil its contracts in the forthcoming year, to justify the fleet it now has and to which it committed itself in the future.
The company stated that, as a result of the government's cutback in expenditure, the Department of Public Works could not clear this obstacle to navigation. Barges travelled downstream at 40 per cent load at a time of year when there was unprecedented development on the Arctic slope and a real opportunity to develop Canada's portion of the Arctic.
I am not blaming the minister; I blame the faceless people in this administration who have not the smallest conception of what transportation in remote areas of Canada means to developing businesses. At a time when we are asserting our sovereignty in the Arctic and trying to develop new resources, the government makes across-the-board cutbacks. No doubt the estimates of the minister's department have been cut back, and as I say I do not blame him. I blame those faceless members in Ottawa who sit in those comfortable pews and have not the slightest idea what is happening in the north.
I want to know just what is happening in the matter of navigation on the Mackenzie

subtopic: STATEMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE, THE HONOURABLE GERARD PELLETIER, TABLED IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS ON NOVEMBER 6, 1969, CONCERNING THE FEDERAL GOVERNMENT'S POLICY WITH RESPECT TO VOLUME II OF THE ROYAL COMMISSION ON BILINGUALISM AND BICULTURALISM

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
I.	GENERAL REMARKS
Over the past few months careful and detailed consideration has been given to those aspects of Volume II of the report of the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Bicul-turalism which are of particular interest to the federal government. Special attention has been devoted to an examination of the extent to which the federal government may be able to assist in this area.
The government acknowledges that much of the substance of the recommendations put forward in Book II is more in the provincial domain than that of the federal government, both in terms of constitutional jurisdiction and as a practical matter. Nevertheless, we believe that there is a dimension to the problem which perforce involves the federal government.
As we see it, this entails the development and encouragement of programs to reinforce and advance the use of the two official languages across the country. More specifically, it relates to twelve of the royal commissioners' recommendations which are addressed directly to the federal government. We also believe that it involves a concerted effort in co-operation with the provinces to ensure that full advantage is taken of the widespread desire, not only to ensure equal rights to the official minority language communities, but also to encourage second-language learning.
The government's basic position is that we accept the principles underlying the recommendations addressed to the federal government and are prepared to provide for a financial contribution to support their implementation. This means that the government is ready to accept its responsibilities as set out by the royal commissioners. It is clear of course that action in this field cannot depend on the federal government alone, for these proposals relate to educational institutions and programmes which are a provincial responsibility. Translation of these principles into practice therefore requires acceptance by the provinces, and beyond that a willingness on their part to take the initiative in putting new programmes into effect.
Secondly, the federal government welcomes and fully supports the view expressed by Canadians that the time has come to provide a better opportunity in Canada, particularly among young people, to learn the second official language, whether this be French or English, as the case may be. We recognize that this would require a concerted effort in the field of education, which is pre-eminently the concern of the provinces, and we will be examining the possibilities for action in this area with the provinces.
Because the government is aware not only of provincial interests but of provincial responsibilities and jurisdiction, our suggestions have been put forward as a basis for discussion and consultation and it is the government's hope that further consideration of the matter can go forward in this spirit. Federal representatives look forward to meeting with their provincial counterparts to work out formulae which will be satisfactory to all concerned.
With respect to financing the programmes involved, the government has indicated that it has no choice but to establish priorities and limitations for all programmes across the range of governmental activities. We have suggested that, realistically, even the best will in the world does not necessarily carry with it the ability to disperse unlimited funds. We have therefore informed the provinces that, after the most careful consideration, the government feels obliged to place at least approximate limits on the amounts which it can contribute to this programme.
II.	RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE ROYAL COMMISSION WHICH ARE ADDRESSED TO THE FEDERAL GOVERNMENT
The twelve recommendations specifically directed to the federal government can be grouped into five categories: the first is recommendation 26 which asserts a general principle; second, recommendation 27 has reference to minority language schools; third, there are four recommendations-numbers 28 and 29, 41 and 42-which have regard to

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
November 6, 1969
teacher-training; fourth, recommendations 23, 24, 25, 30 and 44 are related to university education; and finally, recommendation 46 is concerned with the establishment of a language research council.
a)	General Principle
Recommendation 26 asserts a general proposition to the effect that the federal government should accept, in principle, the responsibility for additional costs involved in official-language minority education. The financial implications of this recommendation and the means of giving substance to this principle are to be found in the remaining recommendations addressed to the federal authority.
b)	Primary and Secondary Schools
Recommendation 27 proposes a formula
which might be used as a basis for establishing costs and the extent of federal financial aid for official-language minority schools. The formula proposed is that a federal grant to provinces be based on the number of students attending official-language minority schools, and that the grant be 10 per cent of the average cost of education per student within the province. The federal government accepts the principle that a grant should be made to provinces for additional costs entailed in providing minority-language education. The government believes, however, that the costing of this recommendation, including the question whether the 10 per cent formula could be applied universally and equitably across the country, svill require further examination and consultation with the provinces.
c)	Teacher-Training
Recommendation 28 proposes a federal grant to Quebec, Ontario and New Brunswick to be based on the number of students attending official-language minority teacher-training institutions, the grant to be 10 per cent of the cost per student plus 10 per cent of capital costs in future. Again, in accordance with the principle that federal government is willing to provide assistance in respect of additional costs arising from minority-language education, we are prepared in principle to accept this recommendation, subject to further discussion of its implications with the provinces.
Recommendation 29 relates to a teachertraining institution at Moncton to service the Western provinces. It suggests that the federal grant to the provinces be 25 per cent of the
cost per student attending each of the two teacher-training institutions. A further recommendation is made that for the Western provinces there be a federal grant covering 75 per cent of capital costs of the institution, and that for the college at Moncton, the grant should cover 50 per cent of capital costs attributable to out-of-province students. The government is prepared to accept this recommendation as a basis for discussion with the provinces, recognizing of course that they may have comments and suggestions regarding numbers of institutions and locations, as well as on the question of financing.
Recommendations 41 and 42 relate to the creation of second-language training centres, designed for the training of language teachers, and to the establishment of an interprovincial bureau of second-language training centres. Recommendation 41 proposes a federal grant to the interprovincial bureau and recommendation 42 suggests that there be a federal-provincial sharing of capital costs of the second-language training centres. The government is prepared to accept the principles embodied in these recommendations and to discuss their implementation with the provinces. In order to give greater encouragement to second-language learning, the government is also prepared to think in terms of a larger number of institutions than that envisaged by the royal commission. Beyond that, we also consider that there may be somehing to be gained by providing for modest bursaries to teachers who would be attending these or similar training institutions, in order to ensure that they would be able to do so without undue hardship. We are prepared to discuss all these aspects with the provinces.
d)	University Education
Recommendation 23 proposes a federal grant to official minority-language students to enable them to study in their own language at a university outside their province when appropriate courses are not offered within the province. The government is ready to accept participation in a programme of this nature and is prepared to discuss the manner of its implementation with the provincial representatives.
Recommendation 24, which should be read in conjunction with recommendation 23, provides for a grant for additional costs that the host university will be expected to incur in respect of visiting students. The commissioners recommend that the grant be equivalent
November 6, 1989

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
to the normal provincial grant to the university. The government is prepared to consider grants for this purpose and to review with the provinces the amounts which might be involved and the manner in which they might be made.
Recommendation 25 proposes that the federal and provincial governments reach agreement on measures required to meet the special needs of French-language universities. In the government's view, this recommendation appears to require special treatment. Our consideration of the matter leads us to believe that it would be difficult to judge the extent of these needs without further study. We have therefore suggested to the provinces that studies be conducted into the nature and dimensions of these needs and the manner of meeting them within available resources. The federal government would be prepared to consider participating in the financing of such studies.
Recommendation 30 proposes that there be a federal grant to provinces in respect of official minority-language universities which would amount to 10% of the provincial grants to these universities. Again, the government is prepared to accept the principle of federal grants for this purpose and to work out the modalities in consultation with the provinces.
Recommendation 44 suggests that the federal government meet the cost of a one-year transfer programme for university students specializing in the second official language. Within limits which will need to be agreed upon, as to the number of students who could be involved in such a programme and the cost per student, the government is prepared to accept this recommendation as well. We would hope to examine the possibilities for such a programme with the provinces.
e)	Language Research Council
Recommendation 46 proposes that a language research council be established by the federal government. We are ready to accept this recommendation and to consult interested parties on the implications of establishing such a council, as well as to the manner in which it could best serve to meet the requirements of improved minority-language education and second-language training.
III.	SECOND-LANGUAGE LEARNING
A study of the recommendations of the commission which are addressed to the federal government shows that they are intended
to cover both minority-language education and second-language learning. The first of these priorities is designed to redress an imbalance which has existed for many years and to ensure access to education in the minority, as well as the majority, language across Canada, wherever this is feasible. The second priority goes beyond this and looks to a future in which there will be an increasing opportunity for all Canadians to learn their second official language.
The government accepts both these priorities, and our acceptance of both is reflected in our willingness to provide financial assistance in both areas in the light of the commission's recommendations. We believe, however, that the further effort which may be required to improve the quality and the quantity of second-language instruction requires experience and knowledge of curricula, facilities and other matters of concern to educators in the provinces. As a result, we believe that further action in this field will require the closest consultation with the provinces on the dimensions of a rational programme in this area, and the means available to meet the needs once the latter are determined.
IV.	FINANCIAL CONSIDERATIONS
Based on our studies, we believe that the recommendations which I have just reviewed can be met, insofar as a federal contribution is concerned, by financial participation in the order of about $50 million for a full year of operations. This amount could increase, within limits established in terms of available resources, as the programme expands with enhanced participation on the part of the provinces. As far as we are concerned, the programme could go into operation in January of next year.
The government naturally envisages a series of further discussions and consultations among federal and provincial representatives on financial aspects of the programme. It was considered desirable, however, to provide a reasonably clear indication at the outset of the limits which financial considerations place on the potential federal contribution.
V.	CONCLUSION
The government regards the problems which have been examined by the royal commissioners, with respect to minority-language education and second-language learning, as being of fundamental significance to the future of Canada. The extent to which the
